s01.slug: MONDAY · 6:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — FRIDAY’S MINE
body: Day twenty-seven. The window over the landing between two and three is still a deep ink blue, with one sodium lamp off the service road caught in its bottom corner like a coal left in a grate, and the tube light over the fourth-floor door is buzzing to itself. The building is asleep in the particular way of a Monday, every door shut on somebody who meant to start the reading Sunday. Jack comes out zipping the Carhartt, on his way down to the Commons for two coffees — his run this week, by an unwritten treaty — and nearly puts his boot through one.

It’s on his step, third down from four, dead center, where he’d have to step over it or into it: a Commons coffee in a brown paper sleeve with the lid on, and under the cup, squared to the edge of the concrete, an index card.

body.title: An index card, under the coffee
body.text: FRIDAY’S MINE. —L.

body: Her capitals. The period, the dash, the L. He picks up the cup and it’s barely warm through the sleeve; she must have been up here a good while ago, in her socks, past his door, and he slept through it. It is his own word from a week ago, said on these stairs about a Saturday, come back to him in her hand and left where he’d trip on it. He has spent three weeks planning things for her — a restaurant with three forks, a bowling alley with his father’s rules — and carrying the plans around in his chest like a man carrying a cake up a ladder. He stands on the step holding a lukewarm coffee and a card, and has no idea what to do with his hands.

He takes it down to her landing anyway. Her step is empty. No index cards, no pencil through a knot of hair, no first sentence going out at the wired glass: only the concrete, and the cold coming off the fire door to two, and the window beginning to go from ink to something you could read by. He sits on her step for a minute and drinks the coffee, which is technically his coffee. It has gone the temperature of the stairwell. The Commons, then.

At half past seven the Commons is steam and trays and the dish return clanking round on its belt, and they’re at the window table: Lena, Laney and Margot, three heads over a yellow legal pad. Laney sees him first. The pad goes face down so fast it lifts a napkin off the table.
“We’re discussing nothing,” Margot says. “At length.”

Lena gets up. She’s in the Saints sweatshirt with a pencil behind her ear and her hair down, and she kisses him quick, hello, coffee and cold air off the lagoon, with one elbow still parked behind her on the legal pad like a paperweight. Somewhere in the middle of the kiss Laney slides the pad out from under the elbow and tucks it under her own arm.
“*Not* on the plans.”

Where the pad was there’s a library book with a white call-number sticker, lying spine-in toward the window. Margot sets her tray on it. Jack doesn’t read the spine. He sits, and takes the index card out of the Carhartt, and puts it down on the table between the cups where all three of them can see it.

Laney studies the ceiling. Margot butters a bagel to the edges and says nothing. Lena picks up her coffee and holds it under her chin in both hands and looks at him over the lid, composed as a hostess at the door of her own party, waiting.
“Somebody left you a note,” she says.
“Somebody left me a coffee. On my step. At six in the morning. Cold.”
“Lukewarm,” Laney says, eyes still up. “It was *hot* when it went up.” Margot kicks her under the table, and Laney adds, with dignity, “I would imagine.”

choices.text: “Is it a parish?”
response: “It’s a *diocese*.”
Margot, with her mouth full: “Archdiocese.”

Lena takes the legal pad back from Laney and turns it over, deliberately, so he can see the back: yellow lines all the way down, not a word, not a doodle. Then she turns it face down again and sets her coffee on it.

choices.text: “You know I don’t want a fuss.”
response: “I know. I’m overruling you.”
Motion carried, at a meeting he wasn’t invited to. She drinks her coffee, and Laney writes something on her napkin and turns it face down too.

choices.text: “Okay. It’s yours.”
response: She had a comeback ready. He watches it go back wherever she keeps them.
She reaches across the cups and takes the index card off the table and puts it in the breast pocket of his flannel herself, under the open Carhartt, and gives the pocket a single pat. “There.”
Her hand takes its time coming away.

s02.slug: MONDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — ET IN ARCADIA
body: Sun on the oak for the first time in a week, coming flat through the half-raised blinds and showing every ring a coffee cup has ever left in the varnish. Jack at the door end under the clock; Lena at the window end with her Waugh open and the spine broken in three places since Sunday; Caleb, Yusuf and the sophomores down the sides with theirs. Somebody’s morning section has left the date on the board in yellow chalk: MARCH 15.
At five past one Hale comes in with *Brideshead* under his arm and the fountain pen clipped in his breast pocket, and sits, and looks at the board.
“The Ides,” he says. “Beware. I always do.”

body.text: Jack sent the word round the table’s email list on Friday, as instructed, and Yusuf has plainly spent the weekend waiting. “Thursday,” he says, to see. Nothing happens. “*Thursday*,” a little louder, and the sophomores look at Hale, and Hale uncaps the pen. “Yes, Mr. Noorzai. It’s a day of the week again. Try not to wear it out.”
body.else: Hale opens the book and, without looking up from it: “The fine on *Thursday* is lifted. I find I have no further use for it.”

body: Book One. They do Oxford. The plovers’ eggs at Sebastian’s lunch; Anthony Blanche at the window with a megaphone, reciting at the rowing men; Aloysius, the bear, who needs a new brush and gets one. “Aloysius is load-bearing,” Yusuf says. “Take him out and the first half comes down.” Hale: “Mr. Noorzai is reading structural engineering into Waugh again. Go on, it’s an improvement.” The sophomore with the nose ring says Charles is in love with Sebastian; another says Charles is in love with being invited; Hale says, “Both, and the second one is England.” They do the picnic under the elms, the strawberries and the wine, and the skull Charles keeps in his rooms in a bowl of roses with the words cut on its forehead, and Hale reads those out, the only words of Waugh’s he reads all hour: *Et in Arcadia ego.* “Even in Arcadia, there am I,” he says. “Death, speaking. At a party. As usual.”

From the window end Lena gives them Sebastian at the picnic, wanting to bury something precious in every place he’s ever been happy, so that when he’s old and ugly and miserable he can come back and dig it up and remember. “He’s twenty years old,” she says, “and he’s already making arrangements to be sad. That’s the most Catholic thing in Book One, and nobody’s said a prayer yet.”
“Miss Broussard finds Catholicism in a picnic.”

“Professor, I’m from New Orleans. I find it in a *parking lot*.” The sophomores laugh. Jack, at the door end, watches her pencil go back behind her ear, and the half smile she gives the oak and not Hale, and thinks he has never wanted to bury anything anywhere, and might start.

Hale sets the pen down and tells the window end and the table at large that the Forum committee has written to him. They would like October. “A rematch,” he says, holding the word away from himself with two fingers. “As though we were heavyweights. I have told them I will accept no other opponent.”
“You didn’t ask me,” Lena says.
“I’m told that’s how it’s done now.”
The sophomores laugh. At the door end Jack looks for something urgent in Waugh.
“And on Thursday,” Hale says, “Miss Broussard has a taste for the floor; she may have mine. You’ll lead, Miss Broussard. Book One. I shall sit where you sit and be insufferable.”
“At the window end?”

“Wherever I like. It’s my table.” He doesn’t smile, and he is very pleased, and the sophomores can see both. Since Thursday night he has stopped pretending to the table that she is merely his best student; he talks to the window end with the proprietary pride of a jockey whose horse threw him.
“I’ll want the pen,” Lena says.
“You will not have the pen.”

Caleb has said nothing since ten past. His pen is capped on his book. When they get to Lord Marchmain — Sebastian’s father, who went abroad years ago and stays there, in Venice, in a palace with a woman who isn’t his wife — Caleb says, to his own page, “Some dads just leave the building.” Nobody answers it. The nose ring goes on about Lady Marchmain’s charm, and the talk moves down the oak and takes the line with it.
With ten minutes left Hale turns his head to the door end. “Mr. Costigan. You’ve been sitting on something since the picnic. Hatch it.”

choices.text: “The bear’s the only thing Sebastian’s honest with.”
response: “Aloysius never lies to him and never asks him down to dinner,” Hale says. “Yes.” He writes something in his own copy with the fountain pen, a short line, and blots it on his cuff.
Across the oak Lena is writing in her margin too, small and fast. From the door end he can’t see what.

choices.text: “Sebastian’s teddy bear has a better wardrobe than I do.”
response: The sophomores laugh. “Everyone at Oxford had a better wardrobe than you, Mr. Costigan,” Hale says. “It was 1923.”
Beside Caleb, Yusuf looks down the table at the Carhartt over the back of Jack’s chair, considers its cuffs, and very quietly nods.

choices.text: “Waugh makes them miserable because he’s about to make them Catholic.”
response: “Spoilers, Mr. Costigan.” Hale turns a page, and can’t leave it there. “He’s not wrong, Miss Broussard. Don’t look so pleased.”

The bell goes in the corridor. Hale says nothing more about any of it while the door end files out past his chair, and Jack goes out with the rest, and is halfway down the Hollis stairs before he notices he’s been let off.

s04.slug: TUESDAY · 11:00 AM · MORRO HALL 1100 — HE ASKED
body: The showers that came through at dawn have gone off east over the hills, and Morro 1100’s long windows are full of a rinsed blue with the lagoon flashing at the bottom of them. Jack climbs the tiers at five to eleven and finds Skye already in the back row under the exit sign, Pair 41, her bag on the floor on her own side.

Her hair is tied up, still damp at the ends, and she’s in a big navy fisherman’s sweater with the cuffs shoved back over her wrists, and she smells of grapefruit, as ever. Jack sits, and gets his notebook out.

“Hi,” she says. She has the pen cap in her teeth. “The moon’s on the sun’s side all week. I looked it up.” She takes the cap out to point it at him. “Did you know the good lows move? In winter they come in the evening. By summer they’re at dawn, and the only people on the reef are surfers and old men with buckets. Textbooks don’t tell you that. A surfer tells you that.”

Down at the board Dr. Fenner has his sun and moon and earth on their string again, three circles in a row. He tells the room what he told it last week, with the same delight: sun and moon pulling the same way, the highest highs of the month, the lowest lows, every day this week. Then he puts the marker down on the tray and turns round and faces the room, which in Jack’s experience he has never done without a slide behind him.
“Last Thursday,” he says, “I asked you to go down to the wharf at Monday evening’s low — the lowest of the month — and look at the pilings.” He looks up the tiers. “Did anybody?”

No one did. A hundred strangers discover something on their phones. Somebody in the fourth row coughs. Fenner waits with his hands in his cardigan pockets, and the hope goes out of his face a little at a time, the way air goes out of a pool float.
From the back row, without standing up, Skye says: “Mussels.”
Every head in Morro 1100 turns round.

“The blue-black ones, in mats, all the way down. Gooseneck barnacles under them — they look like a bunch of tiny hooves. Ochre stars, orange and purple, five or six to a piling. Anemones closed up like fists, because they were out of the water and they didn’t like it. And the waterline was a foot below where it was last Thursday.” She holds the white iPhone up toward the front of the room, eighty feet off, with a picture on it too small to make out past the third row.
Fenner takes his glasses off. He holds them down at his side and looks up the tiers at the back row with his bare face, and he is so happy that for a while he can’t do anything with it.

“Pair forty-one,” he says finally. “Thank you.” He puts the glasses back on. “*Pollicipes polymerus*. They feed with their legs. Upside down. All their lives.” He turns back to the board and finds the marker, and the whole room can hear him humming.
Jack leans over. “You went last Thursday too.”

“I needed a control.” She thumbs between two pictures of the same piling: the same black ruff of mussels, the same orange star, and the wet line on the wood a foot lower in the second. “Monday it was at six-something. Tonight it’s fifty minutes later. I’m going to keep going till it’s the middle of the night, and then I’m going to stop being interested.” She scrolls to a third picture: a man in a county windbreaker on the wharf, frowning straight into the lens. “He thought I was from the state. I let him. He showed me a sea slug.”

Down at the board Fenner is still humming, and she watches him with the pen cap back in her teeth, and then — briefly, low, for Jack only — she is a woman in a housecoat at a dinner table somewhere in the Valley, passing the peas. “*Dale.* Honey. Somebody looked at the pilings.” A sniff. “I always said somebody would.” And she’s back, copying the tide table off the board.
She flips back a page for him. In last week’s margin there’s PILINGS, in her capitals, boxed. He reaches over and puts a check beside it in his pencil.
Skye looks at the check. “I was wrong about him,” she says. “That’s going to bother me all week.”

At the half hour Fenner comes up the side stairs with the refraction projects in a stack, ticking pairs on his clipboard. At theirs he stops, and asks Pair forty-one, if they would be so kind, for a page on the pilings by Thursday — the first optional assignment anybody can remember him setting — and lays the project on the desk and goes on down the row: the graph paper, the Point traced off the chart, the four colors of wave bending onto the reef. In the corner, in Fenner’s red ballpoint, *Both halves. Good.* And under it, circled, an A.
She doesn’t say anything. She points at it.
“We got an A,” he says.
“*I* got an A. You got the math.” She slides the sheet into a folder, carefully, flat, without bending it. “The math got a B-plus. I’m being generous.”
For the rest of the hour they take down the tides side by side, the rinsed light moving down the long windows. He takes notes on the Coriolis effect as though his life depended on it.
At a quarter past twelve the room comes apart down the tiers in zippers and backpacks. She puts the folder in her bag and stands up with the bag on her shoulder.
“Did you bring proofs?”
“Tomorrow.”
“Bring the good ones,” Skye says. “I read ahead again.”

choices.text: “I’m bringing five. Aquinas did the lifting; I’m just carrying them.”
choices.key: When Skye asked if you were bringing proofs, you told her you’d bring Aquinas’s five and carry them yourself.
response: “Then I’ll be ready for five.” She caps her pen with her teeth and drops it in the bag.
The Saab key is already in her hand by the time she reaches the side door at the bottom of the tiers, and the door has swung shut behind her before he has his notebook closed.

choices.text: “I’ve got two I believe and three I can recite.”
choices.key: When Skye asked if you were bringing proofs, you told her you had two you believed and three you could recite.
response: “Bring the two.” She looks at him over the top of the phone. “The three I can get off Wikipedia.”
She goes up the aisle against the crowd coming down for the 12:30, the only person in the building going the wrong way, and the crowd parts for her without seeming to notice it’s doing it.

choices.text: “I’m bringing the one that got me.”
choices.key: When Skye asked if you were bringing proofs, you told her you’d bring the one that got you.
response: “Which one got you?”
“Ask me at four.”
It goes all through her face, and she doesn’t say a word about it, and then she’s gone down the side stairs, and Jack is alone in Pair 41 with the A.

s05.slug: TUESDAY · 10:20 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE WALK-IN
body: The Anchor’s back kitchen at twenty past ten smells of bleach and fryer oil and, under them tonight, something sweet and licorice that doesn’t belong to anything on the menu. Tuesday is the slow night: four booths, two fishermen, a table of nursing students splitting fries, and the Hobart with nothing to do but wait for him. Jack comes in through the back door from the dumpster with the empty bins in one hand and the Carhartt still on against the wind off the wharf, and Rudy, at the flattop with his scraper and his radio going low in Spanish on the shelf above him, says before Jack has opened his mouth: “Mijo. I know nothing.”
Jack hasn’t asked him anything.
Gloria comes through from the front with the coffee pot, past the dish station, past Jack, past the walk-in, and does not break stride. “You didn’t see anybody in my walk-in.”

He hadn’t. He does now. The walk-in door has a porthole in it the size of a dinner plate, fogged at the edges, and through the clear middle of it is the Saints sweatshirt with one of Rudy’s white aprons tied twice round it, standing over a fifty-pound sack of flour on the floor with a clipboard, and a jar of anise seed on the shelf at her elbow among the butter. On the steel table by the ovens two small loaves are cooling on a sheet pan, one gold, the other dark as a saddle all down the end that faced the back.
“The back of the oven runs hot,” Rudy says, scraping. “I told her.”

The walk-in door opens on its gasket. Lena comes out with the clipboard against her chest and flour to the elbows and a streak of it in her eyebrow, sees him standing there with a bin in each hand, and stops. Since September he has never seen anyone go into that walk-in who wasn’t paid to, and she stops dead: chin up, eyes going once to the swinging door Gloria went out by. Then she crosses the tile and puts one floury hand flat on his chest, to hold him exactly where he is, and kisses him, by the Hobart, the cold of the walk-in still coming off her.

“You didn’t see me,” she says against his mouth, and goes back in, and pulls the walk-in door shut behind her with both hands. Through the porthole she turns her back on him and makes a mark on the clipboard.
There is a white handprint on the front of the Carhartt over his ribs, five fingers and a palm. He looks at it, and leaves it.
Gloria comes back through with the empty pot, looks at the handprint, looks at the walk-in door, and says to the coffee machine, “I didn’t see that either.”

He does an hour at the dish machine with his hands bare, a week after Kevin told him what that does to them. Every time the walk-in door sighs on its gasket behind him he doesn’t turn round, which takes more out of him than the dishes do. Once, Rudy goes in with a hotel pan and comes out without it, and passes Jack on the way back to the grill, and says, without stopping, “The anise is for a cake. For my sister,” and Jack says, “Okay, Rudy,” and Rudy looks relieved to have got that settled.
At a quarter to eleven he takes a rack of clean cups out front, and Laney Price is sitting at the counter by herself.

He has never seen Laney at the Anchor without an audience. She is in a pink velour sweatsuit with her hair up in a scrunchie, which is how Laney dresses when there’s been a death, and she has a slice of coconut cream in front of her that she has not touched, and when she sees him she points her fork at him across the Formica.
He puts the cups down on the counter by the coffee station and doesn’t sit.

“A soprano in the Newman band,” Laney says, “the tall one who does the descant at Communion like somebody’s paying her by the note — she sat down next to me on the lagoon steps tonight and asked was I *okay*, because of *Kevin*. And I said why on God’s green earth wouldn’t I be okay about Kevin. And she told me.” The fork comes down an inch. “Clare. A *week* ago. In the Newman kitchen.” She jerks her fork at the register. “And *Gloria* says he came in here after. Tuesday. Your *shift*.” At the register Gloria becomes very interested in a roll of receipt paper. “You *knew*. A *week*.”
“He asked me not to.”

Something goes over her face, furious and touched in the same breath, and she can’t pick, so she does both. “You *kept* it. Of course you kept it. You keep *everything*, you’re like a — you’re a *safe-deposit box* in a flannel shirt.” She puts the fork down and picks it back up. “I bought him a slice. I was going to take it to 420.” She looks at the slice. “Was he okay? When he came in?”
Jack thinks about the counter a week ago, the good quarter-zip zipped to the collarbone, the fork lined up beside the saucer. “He had the coconut cream,” he says. “All of it.”

Laney puts her hand over her mouth. “He *always* gets the toast,” she says through it. “He gets the toast and he holds everybody’s keys.” She takes the hand down. “He’s been doing his picture smile all week, at breakfast, at Mass, and I thought it was a *test*.” She stabs at the crust and doesn’t eat it. “And I *liked* her. She fixed his collar in church. Now I have to be *civil* to her at the sign of peace till we graduate.” And smaller: “Did he say anything about *me*?”
“He said you’d organize something.”
Laney sits back on the stool and closes her eyes.

“Sugar,” she says, “I am going to organize *everything*.” Her eyes open. “There is going to be a casserole rota on that boy’s door by breakfast. Through *Easter*. Tuna noodle. King Ranch. Margot is going to make whatever it is Swedish people make when they’re sad. He is going to be *fed*, and he’s going to be *visited*, and he is never going to eat alone in a diner at midnight again for as long as I draw breath.”
“Tuna noodle he gets from me,” Gloria says from the register, to the receipt paper. “With the potato chips on top.”

“Gloria, you’re on call.” Laney doesn’t even look round. “Where was I. *Fed*. And Friday he’s getting fed whether he likes it or —” She stops. She looks at the kitchen door. “Friday’s nothing. Forget Friday.”
Behind the pass, Rudy turns his radio up.

choices.text: “He asked me not to tell you. So I didn’t.”
choices.key: When Laney found out about Kevin and Clare and came to the Anchor, you told her you’d kept it because he asked you to.
response: “I *know*,” Laney says. “That’s what makes me so *mad*.”

She stabs the coconut cream. Then she eats it — Kevin’s slice, the one she bought to carry up four flights in a napkin — furiously, in big bites, the whole thing to the last crumb of crust, glaring at Jack the entire time as if it were his fault the pie was good.

choices.text: “He’s going to need a spreadsheet.”
choices.key: When Laney found out about Kevin and Clare and came to the Anchor, you told her Kevin was going to need a spreadsheet.
response: “He’s going to *get* one. Color-coded. He’s going to hate it, and it is going to be *so good* for him.”

She has three pens out of her purse before she’s done saying it, pink and green and black, and pulls a napkin out of the dispenser and starts ruling it into columns. MON. TUE. WED. Jack goes back to the kitchen for the next rack. When he comes out again she’s on her third napkin and has gotten as far as Holy Week.

choices.text: *Let her be angry at you. It’s easier for her than being sad for him.*
choices.key: When Laney found out about Kevin and Clare and came to the Anchor, you let her be angry at you instead.
response: He stands there with his macerated hands at his sides and takes all of it — the safe-deposit box, the week, every breakfast he sat across from her and said *pass the salt* like a *Methodist* — and she runs out of angry before her coffee has gone cold.

Then she orders a whole coconut cream pie to go, for 420. Gloria boxes it without being asked and ties the string twice. Laney goes out the door with the box held level in both hands in front of her, chin up, not crying, and the bell rings over her.

s06.slug: WEDNESDAY · 7:15 AM · DELGADO HALL, HER LANDING — CABBAGES
body: The legal pad must be finished, because she’s back on her step: sweatpants, wool socks, a cereal bowl on her knees full of dried chickpeas, and she is going through them one at a time with a fingertip, pushing them from one side of the bowl to the other, picking out the little stones and the split ones and dropping them in a coffee cup on the step beside her. *Plink*, goes a stone into the cup. The window over her head has the morning in it, pale and clear, with a contrail crossing it.
The RAZR in his breast pocket has a text on it from while he was shaving.

body.text: ERIN GO BRAGH. WEAR GREEN OR YOUR MOTHER WILL HEAR ABOUT IT.

body: The Costigans are Frank’s side, the Irish half, and every March 17 his father remembers it for one day and texts like the owner of a pub. Jack has his green flannel on already. He isn’t about to find out what his mother would hear.
Lena looks at the flannel and then holds up a chickpea to it, judicially, for color.

“In New Orleans,” she says, “on St. Patrick’s, they have a parade down Magazine Street through the Irish Channel, and the men on the floats throw *cabbages*. Whole heads. And potatoes, and carrots, and onions, off a moving truck, at people. And if you catch a cabbage, you go home and make corned beef and cabbage, and that’s your supper, and it’s a miracle, because you were struck by it.” She drops a stone in the cup. “Jude caught one in the face when he was six, and Mama says it explains a great deal.” She is not Irish, and she says all of this with the authority of somebody who has been hit by produce for the faith.

She has the paper off the lobby rack folded under the bowl, open to the inside pages, the health-care bill again. The Catholic hospitals are for it. The bishops are against it, because of what it would pay for. She taps the two columns with a fingernail, one and then the other. “I can’t decide who I’m angrier at. The sisters who run half the hospitals from here to Shreveport say pass it and the poor get a doctor. The bishops say not one dime for abortion, so no. And I agree with *both* of them, Jack, which is a sin against something, I just haven’t found out what.”
“Stupak’ll fold by Sunday.”
“He will *not*.” She shakes a chickpea at him. “That man has a spine like a pew.”

He has his four-dollar Catechism under his arm, and folded into it at thirty-one, sticking out an inch, two sheets of notebook paper covered on both sides in pencil. Proofs, or what he could get onto two pages between the end of his shift and two in the morning. She sees them. Her eyes go to the folded corners, and then back up to his face.
She doesn’t wish him luck, or make anything of four o’clock.
“Tell me after.”
“I will.”

She nods, and looks down, and goes back to the chickpeas. He stands on the step above her and watches her hands go through the bowl, the right one sorting and the left one holding the rim steady, sure and quick and careful, turning each one over before she lets it stay.

s07.slug: WEDNESDAY · 4:00 PM · LOW TIDE, LAS OLAS — QUESTION THE SEA
body: The showers have blown through by three, and Las Olas has come out wet and shining under a sun that won’t make up its mind. Two blocks over, St. Patrick’s Day is already loud: a bagpipe being learned on a porch, green plastic bowlers hung on the bike racks, a boy in a shamrock bodysuit asleep face-down on a lawn at four in the afternoon. A block in from Seacliff Road it’s quieter. Low Tide is the way he left it a week ago: the old racks up the walls with their three yellowed longboards, the menu painted on a fourth, the varnished plywood counter, DOLORES on her Post-it on the espresso machine, the barista with the nose ring. The two surfers in hoodies are at the table under the racks, arguing, as far as Jack can tell, the same swell.

There’s a board in the short rack by the back door, the one that has stood empty for as long as Low Tide has been a coffee shop: a battered single-fin with the wax gone brown and a ding in the nose patched with something white, and it’s still dripping on the concrete.
“First board in that rack in ten years,” the barista tells him, unasked, snapping a lid onto somebody’s to-go cup, and tips her head at the back table.

Skye is already there, at the table by the long window, and she’s wet. She has come straight out of the water. The wetsuit is peeled down to her waist, black neoprene with the arms knotted round her hips, and above it she has on a green bikini top that is plainly a swimsuit and plainly not anything anybody has ever worn to a coffee shop. The salt is drying white on her shoulders and in her hair, down and long and sun-streaked and tangled, and still dripping on the binder in front of her. There’s sand on her ankles and on the concrete under the chair. A towel hangs round her neck. She’s barefoot. She has a surfer’s shoulders, which he had somehow forgotten, and the freckles have come out across her nose. It’s the girl he went out to the Point with at dawn, and it doesn’t look like a costume at all.
The barista comes round the end of the counter with a second towel and drops it on the back of Skye’s chair in passing, like a refill. Skye throws it over her own shoulder, on top of the first one.
One of the surfers tips his chair back on two legs. “Sands?”
“Waist-high,” Skye says. “Glassy till eleven. Then the wind.”
Both of them nod, deep and respectful. The one on two legs lets his chair down. “On the single-fin?”
“I’m old-fashioned.”
He thinks about this and approves of it, and turns the approval on Jack, who is standing there in a Carhartt with a four-dollar Catechism under his arm. “You surf, bro?”
“I’m from Ohio.”
“Oh.” Real sympathy. “Sorry, man.” And they go back to their argument.
Jack sits down. There’s a coffee on his side of the table already, black, in the mug with the chip out of the handle.

body.text: “I kept it,” she says, of nothing he can see, and nothing more.

body: “It’s the only green I own,” Skye says. “It’s St. Patrick’s. I’m observant.” She wrings a rope of hair out over the floor, well away from the book, and from the counter the barista sends a third towel sliding down the plywood after it. “Last week was wardrobe. This is just what I look like at four o’clock if nobody makes me change.” She lets him have about a second of that. “That’s a lie. It’s a strategy. It’s a very good strategy.”

body.text: She looks at his Carhartt, buttoned to the second snap, and down at her own bare shoulders. “Last week you told me I was overdressed. I took the note.” A drop runs off the end of her hair and down the inside of her arm. “So. Now who’s underdressed?”

body: He looks. There isn’t a version of the next minute in which he doesn’t, and his body answers the line of her collarbone and the wet green of the swimsuit all at once and frankly, before the rest of him has been asked.

body: For ten minutes it’s Oceanography. Fenner’s page on the pilings is due tomorrow, and she has written her half in her small fast capitals and wants his. The refraction project from Tuesday is in her folder with its red A in the corner. She takes it out long enough to say, “An A’s a grade. It isn’t a review,” and puts it back. She reads his paragraph on the gooseneck barnacles, crosses out *weird* and writes *sessile*, and slides it back to him.

body.text: Before the book, she sits back with the two towel ends in her fists. “I said I’d turn it over till Friday,” she says. “I turned it over till Saturday.” She looks out at the bike path. “A God who doesn’t need anything from me. I’ve never been in a room with anybody like that. I don’t know how you’d play it.” And she opens the binder.

Before the book, she sits back with the two towel ends in her fists. “I turned that over all week,” she says. She looks out at the bike path. “A God who doesn’t need anything from me. I’ve never been in a room with anybody like that. I don’t know how you’d play it.” And she opens the binder.

Before the book, she puts another paperback on the table beside it: the *Confessions*, a Penguin, the spine already broken in two places. “Two books in,” she says. “He’s very upset about a pear.” She puts it away and opens the binder.
Before the book, she taps its cover with one finger. “You said you can’t prove it, you believe it. I want to see if that holds up once there are proofs on the table.” She opens the binder.

body: The binder is open to the tab KNOWING, and the three highlighters lie along the top of it in their row: yellow, she agrees; pink, she doesn’t; green, a good line. The book is beside it, the Borders sticker going soft at one corner. She turns the pages on past the end of last week.

body.text: On the way past twenty-seven he catches START LOOKING, still in its box across the top of the page, and under it, new, in green, smaller: *still looking.*

body: The receipt is in the gutter at thirty-one. Down the page, *converging and convincing arguments* has gone yellow. A line above it *proofs* is pink, with a question mark in the margin the size of a fishhook.
“In my business,” she says, “‘convincing’ is a note you give an actor who isn’t.”

body.text: “Five,” she says, and holds out her hand across the plywood. He unfolds the two sheets out of the Catechism and she counts down them with one wet finger — motion, cause, contingency, degrees, design — five, as advertised, and hands them back. “Aquinas did the lifting. You did the carrying. I checked.” She taps the third one. “Keep that one out. I’m going to want it.”

“The two,” she says, before he can get them out, and holds out her hand. He unfolds the sheets out of the Catechism. She skips the three he can recite — she can tell which they are; they’re the neat ones — and reads the two that have been crossed out and written over, the margins gone gray with eraser. “These,” she says. “The ones that fought back. Those are the ones I came for.”

“It’s four,” she says. He looks at her. “You said ask you at four. Which one got you?” He doesn’t unfold the sheets. “That there’s anything at all,” he says. “When there didn’t have to be. That one got me, and it never let go.” She looks at him a second longer than the answer needs, and nods once, and doesn’t write it down.

body: She moves her finger down a paragraph to thirty-two, where the book hands the floor to Augustine, and reads it off the page: *Question the beauty of the sea.*
“So I did,” Skye says. “For two hours. I’m reporting back.”

choices.text: “You’re dripping on the desire for God.”
response: “You’re dripping on the desire for God.”
“The desire for God was *last* week. Keep up.” She moves the book an inch out of range, and leaves the hair where it is.

choices.text: “How was it out there?”
response: “How was it out there?”
“Perfect.” She looks down at the book when she says the rest. “That’s my problem.”
She says it to the paragraph, so it’s the argument she means, mostly. He hears the rest of it anyway.

choices.text: *Look at the page.*
response: He looks at the page. Thirty-one, the receipt, her pink fishhook. He reads it to the bottom and goes on into thirty-two, while a drop off the end of her hair lands on the plywood beside his hand.
“Coward,” she says, pleasantly, and turns the book round to face him at thirty-one.
His eyes stay on the print. Eventually, a sentence or two along, he is actually reading it.

body: She paddled out at Sands at half past one, she says, after the wind came up and everybody else came in, and sat past the break for two hours on the board in the chop, and came straight here, and did exactly what it says. She asked. She tells it to him straight across the table with her elbows on the binder.

“I looked at it for two hours. The light on it. The way a set comes in and the first wave’s never the best one, so you wait. A harbor seal came up next to the board twice and looked at me like I was in its seat. Pelicans went over so low I could hear the air in them. At about two-fifteen the sun came out on the water all at once, a mile wide. I looked at it like it was somebody across a table I was trying to read.” She stops. “It was beautiful every single time, and it didn’t say a word. It wasn’t saying anything. I was.”
“In the wind?” he says. “Everybody else had come in.”

“The wind was the point. Anybody thinks a glassy morning’s beautiful. I wanted to see if it still was when it was ugly.” “It was. That’s what bothers me. It was gorgeous while it was trying to drown me.”
Behind her, through the long window, past the bike path and the ice plant and the lifeguard tower, there’s a strip of it, blue going to green, with the sun on it in pieces.

“Here’s what I think it is,” she says. “We’re animals. For about a hundred thousand years the people who liked the look of water and a long horizon lived near the fish and the fresh water, and they could see who was coming, and they had kids. The ones who didn’t care for the view didn’t do as well. I’m descended from a very long line of people who thought the ocean was gorgeous.” She points the capped end of the yellow highlighter at the window. “So of course it feels like a message. It *is* one. It’s from my great-great-everybody, and it says *stay near the fish*. The beauty’s in the wiring. That’s exactly why it feels like somebody’s talking. Same with fire. Same with a baby’s face. Same with a sunset, which is just the air being dirty in the right direction.”

She picks the Catechism up and holds it to her ear like a telephone, and she’s a recorded surf line, a voice Jack has never heard in his life and knows anyway: a man who has been awake since four and stoned since five, reading the report off a napkin.

“*Thanks for calling the Sands surf report. Motion: steady. Becoming: waist to chest. Contingency: high.*” A long, contented pause, full of static. “*Order and beauty: glassy all morning, blown out by noon.*”

Still on the phone, still in it, as slow as the tide: “And if everything needs a reason, so does yours. Who made him? Don’t say *nobody*. If *nobody* is allowed, I’ll take it for the sea and save us a step.” She hangs the book up on the table. “Beep.”

It’s a good one, and an old one, the one every kid asks in second grade and Hume made respectable. And she isn’t wrong about the water. He was eighteen before he ever saw an ocean, and on the first morning, at a pull-off on Route 1 beside his father’s truck, he felt spoken to, and couldn’t have told anybody who was doing the talking. Before that it was Lake Erie, which is big and brown and nobody calls it beautiful to its face. It seemed to him that first morning the most obvious thing in the world that somebody had meant it. It still does. The trouble is that she has just told him exactly why it would.

choices.text: *Contingency — not who knocked over the first domino. What’s holding the line up right now.*
response: “Everything you sat on for two hours might not have been,” he says. “The wave, the board, you. Things that might not be don’t explain why they are. Something has to be that can’t not be, or there’d be nothing at all. That’s Aquinas. That isn’t who started it. It’s who’s holding it up this afternoon.”
“Or it’s just there,” she says at last. “No reason. Brute. Some things are.”
“Then you’re the one stopping at the sea. Not me.”
She doesn’t answer that. Her hair drips on the open page, and a dark spot spreads slowly over *contingency*, and she lets it.

choices.text: *The sea isn’t the speaker. It’s the letter.*
response: “Augustine never says the sea talks,” he says. “Read the next line. *Their beauty is a profession* — and the book puts the Latin in brackets, *confessio*. A confession. Somebody else’s. You don’t ask a letter what it thinks. You ask who wrote it.”
“Letters get forged.”
“Then somebody forged it. Still somebody.”
“Huh,” she says.
She turns in her chair and looks out the long window at the strip of blue past the bike path, a long look, the same one she gave it for two hours.

choices.text: “You’re right that *nobody* is allowed. The book doesn’t say you can’t stop at the sea. It says you won’t.”
response: “You’re right that *nobody* is allowed,” he says. “The book doesn’t say you can’t stop at the sea. It says you won’t. Thirty-four says the world doesn’t have its own first principle in it, or its own last end. It’s betting on you. You’ll keep asking why there’s a sea. If you can stop asking, you win.”
She’s quiet. Then: “I can’t stop asking. You know I can’t.”

choices.text: “Two hours on a board to test one paragraph. Augustine would’ve hired you.”
response: “Two hours on a board to test one paragraph. Augustine would’ve hired you.”

“Augustine couldn’t *afford* me.” The delight gets to her face first and the argument gets there second. “I’d have charged him by the paragraph. Thirteen books about himself. He’d have been good for it.”

body: Thirty-three, and she’s on her feet before he’s finished reading it, barefoot on the concrete with one towel swung round her shoulders like a shawl, and she’s somebody else: a woman in a caftan and a great many bracelets who teaches a Saturday class in a converted dry cleaner’s in Studio City and has not sat down since 1979.

“*Openness!*” she tells the shop, clapping on the beat. “From the *diaphragm!* *Truth and beauty* — find it in the pelvis, people, it is not in your *face!* *Moral goodness* — on the out-breath! *Freedom* — shake out your hands! And *conscience*” — she wheels on Jack, bracelets and all — “where does it *live?* *Show* me!”
Behind the counter the barista says “*Yes*.” One of the surfers says, over his shoulder, “My sister took that class,” and goes back to his argument. Skye sits down.
She puts the towel back round her neck and holds both ends of it, and looks at the binder instead of at him.

“I know whose voice my conscience has,” she says. “It’s my mother’s. It says *again*, and *smile*, and *they’re not paying you to have a face like that.*” A drop of water runs out of her hair and down the side of her neck, and she leaves it. “I’ve had Debbie’s voice in my head since I was eleven. You’d call it God’s. I know exactly which lot she parks in.”
“What does it say when you get it right?”
“It doesn’t. That’s how you know you got it right.”

The surfers argue on under the racks. The stereo goes on into the next song. Jack has his pencil in his hand and nothing to do with it. He knows Debbie the way you know the weather in another state: by what it has done to the person who just drove in from there. His own conscience talks in Ma’s voice about half the time — *Did you eat? Don’t lie to me* — and in a nun’s the rest. But under both of them there has always been something else that doesn’t sound like anybody, and that he has never been able to do an impression of.

“That’s all it is,” she says, more quietly. “Whoever raises you puts a voice in. Later you hear it and think it came down through the ceiling. Some kids get a nice one.” She turns the book round to him and puts her finger at the end of thirty-three, on the line about the soul: *the seed of eternity we bear in ourselves, irreducible to the merely material.* “And this. I can make a whole theater believe there’s somebody in here. It’s my job. A soul’s the oldest special effect there is.”

He thinks of Nonna at Christmas in the front room on Glenwood, who couldn’t always say which grandson he was, and who knew to the day how many Sundays were left before Lent. Somebody in there was keeping the calendar. He would bet the house on it. He can’t prove it to a girl who can make a whole theater believe in somebody who isn’t there.

choices.text: *The debunking saws off its own branch — and Debbie never asked whether a line was true.*
response: “If your conscience is only Debbie,” he says, “so is the voice telling you it’s only Debbie. You don’t get to trust the one that tells you not to trust it. Some of it’s her. Not the part that asks whether it’s *true*.” He leans in over the plywood. “Last week you asked me whether a line was true or just a line. Debbie never asked you that in your life. She wanted it to land.”
“Maybe that part’s just me,” she says.
“Then it’s you. It isn’t Debbie. That’s all I need.”
Skye looks at him for a good while. “That’s annoyingly good,” she says, to the towel.

choices.text: *“You cried in a parking garage the day you got everything you wanted. That’s the longing for the infinite.”*
response: “You cried in a parking garage the day you got everything you wanted,” he says. “That’s the longing for the infinite. You told me so, at this table.”
She looks at the window, and back at him, level. “I told you that as a *story*.”
“I know.”
“Okay.” She writes something in pink and tips the binder so he can’t see it. Her face has gone very still and very friendly.

choices.text: “You’re right that some of it’s her. Mine’s got Ma in it, and Nonna, and a nun at St. Brigid’s with a yardstick.”
response: “You’re right that some of it’s her,” he says. “Mine’s got Ma in it, and Nonna, and a nun at St. Brigid’s with a yardstick. The book doesn’t say conscience comes to you clean. It says it comes.”
“A yardstick,” she says. “That’s so much worse than a ruler. Did it work?”
“On the knuckles, every time.”
“That’s so much worse.” And then, straight across the table: “Thank you for not telling me she’s God.”

choices.text: “If your conscience is your mother, mine’s mine. And mine would eat yours.”
response: “If your conscience is your mother, mine’s mine,” he says. “And mine would eat yours.”
“She’d *try*. Debbie’s undefeated.” Skye grins and doesn’t bother hiding it. “Put them in a room. I’d pay.”
Jack laughs, and she takes it like applause, one small nod to the house.

body: “— no, because look at thirty-seven.” She’s already turning the book round to him across the plywood, her finger under the line before he’s found it: *persuade themselves that what they would not like to be true is false or at least doubtful.* “People who don’t believe are people who don’t *want* to. That’s last week’s move with footnotes. Fine. Then you’re a person who *does* want to.” She turns her hand over on the table, palm up, palm down. “It cuts exactly as deep both ways, and your book only swings it in one direction.”
“That isn’t what it —”
“I’m not done.”

She flips back two pages without looking. “And this one admits it. Thirty-five. The proofs can *predispose* you. That’s what a doctor says about a family history.” She taps the word. “The proofs get you to a *first cause*. Nobody ever lit a candle for a first cause. You need him to show up and *say* something.” She goes back to thirty-seven. “And this list. Why it’s hard to see him. The senses, the imagination, and — my favorite — *disordered appetites*.” She looks at him over the top of the book. “Your church has a footnote for being hungry for the wrong thing. I think that’s the most honest sentence in the chapter.” Jack, sitting across from a girl in a bikini top, is not at this moment the man to argue with her about disordered appetites, and from her face she’s aware of it. She runs her finger down to thirty-eight. “And then it just says so. Man needs to be *enlightened by God’s revelation*. You can’t get there on your own steam. So the proofs are the warm-up. They’re the caftan lady.” She sits back. “I respect that, actually. I respect a script that knows where its hole is.”
“Thirty-six says reason gets there with *certainty*,” he says. “That’s a lot for a book to claim before it admits it needs help.”

“Certain *what*, though? Certain there’s a first cause. That’s like being certain there’s a writer because there’s a script.” She shrugs. “Great. Is he any good? Does he know my name? Is he going to give me notes?”
“That’s the difference between knowing *that* and knowing *who*.”
“That’s a writers’-room distinction. I’ve been in writers’ rooms. They make those up at two in the morning so nobody has to go home.”

The sun has gone long on the bike path, and the bikes going by throw their shadows in across the floor and out again. One of the surfers has left. The other has his hood up and his eyes shut and may or may not be listening.

She’s right about thirty-seven, and he knows it from the inside. He has talked himself out of God for an hour at a time on bad nights, because an hour without him would have been easier. It never lasted, and it never felt like thinking. He isn’t sure that proves what he’d like it to.

And then she sits up very straight in the plastic chair, and lays one hand on the open book to swear on it, and is, as far as Jack can tell, a council father at the Vatican in 1870, an old one, with a cold, in a heavy Latin English that carries every syllable in on a cushion: “*God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known — with certainty — from the created world — by the natural light of human* —”
She drops it on the last word like a hot plate.
“— reason. Great. So where’s Chapter Two?”

choices.text: *If wanting cuts both ways, it can’t decide anything.*
choices.key: When Skye said wanting it to be true cut both ways, you told her that was exactly why it couldn’t settle anything — the argument was still on the table.
response: “You’re right, it cuts both ways,” he says. “So it can’t settle anything. If I believe because I want to and you don’t because you don’t, that’s two biographies. Lewis has a name for it — explaining why the other guy thinks what he thinks before you’ve shown he’s wrong. The argument’s still sitting on the table where we left it, and somebody has to answer it.”
“What’s the name?”
“Bulverism.”
“That’s a terrible name. It sounds like something cattle get.”
Skye puts one finger down on the plywood between the two mugs, where the argument is, and holds it there while she thinks.

choices.text: “The proofs get you to the door. They don’t open it. The book says so itself.”
choices.key: When Skye said the proofs only got you to a first cause, you granted that they get you to the door, and that the book says so itself.
response: “The proofs get you to the door,” he says. “They don’t open it. The book says so itself. That’s why there’s a Chapter Two.”
“A door.” She turns ahead to thirty-nine, and back to thirty-five. “Okay. I’ll take a door.”
Her thumb finds the receipt in the gutter and rests on it, and she sits like that a while, with her door.

choices.text: *Tell her the truth about wanting.*
choices.key: When Skye said you believed because you wanted to, you told her that if you believed what you wanted, you’d believe a lot less of it.
response: “If I believed what I wanted, Skye, I’d believe a lot less of it.”
That’s all of it. He leaves it on the table.
She looks at him for a long time across the plywood, with the low light on one side of her face.
“That’s the first thing you’ve said that I believe completely.”
Her pen is lying on the open book where she put it down. She leaves it there.

choices.text: “You want Chapter Two. That’s the most promising thing anybody’s said at this table.”
choices.key: When Skye asked where Chapter Two was, you told her wanting it was the most promising thing anyone had said at that table.
response: “You want Chapter Two,” he says. “That’s the most promising thing anybody’s said at this table.”

“Don’t get *excited*.” But she’s laughing, and she tips the binder up so he can see the margin by thirty-eight, where at some point in the last five minutes she has drawn a small door, in green, with a knob. “I don’t trust a door without a knob,” she says.

s07d.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:40 PM · LOW TIDE — BRING ADJECTIVES
body: Past half five the cloud lifts off the water and the sun comes in under it, straight down the length of the shop, and lays the shadows of the board racks across the concrete like a fence. Her hair is nearly dry, gone stiff and pale with salt, and the sand under her chair has dried to powder. Thirty-eight is done. She sits back in the plastic chair.

body.text: “Draw,” she says. “The director’s awake this time, and he still couldn’t pick.” She opens the back cover and writes DRAW inside it, in pink.
“Fine,” she says, to the book, and then to him. “Roman numerals two and three to you.”
“The two biographies. That one’s going in green.”
“Debbie and the line. I’m going to hear that every time she calls.”
“The thing holding it up this afternoon. I’ll be thinking about that out past the break.”
“The letter, and who wrote it. That was good. I’m furious.”
“Mine,” she says. “And I didn’t even need the wetsuit.” She opens the back cover and writes the score inside it in green, and underlines it.
“The parking garage was a cheap shot,” she says. “It worked. I hate that it worked.”
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *COSTIGAN 2 — SKYE 0.* “Breathe through your nose,” she says, before he can.
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *COSTIGAN 1 — SKYE 1.* “Now it’s a *show*.”
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *COSTIGAN 1 — SKYE 0 — DRAW 1.* “That’s a lead. Barely.”
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *COSTIGAN 1 — DRAW 1.* “Wipe that off your face. It doesn’t suit you.”

Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *DRAW 2.* “The director’s on a *bender*.”
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *SKYE 1 — COSTIGAN 1.* “Now it’s a *show*.”
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *SKYE 2 — COSTIGAN 0.* “Next week I’ll go easy on you.” A beat. “I won’t.”
Along the bottom of the back cover she keeps the running total. She writes it now, small: *SKYE 1 — COSTIGAN 0 — DRAW 1.* “Still mine. Barely.”

body: She takes the receipt out of the gutter at thirty-one and moves it on, past the end of thirty-eight, and turns the book round to him with one finger under the heading of thirty-nine: *How Can We Speak about God?*
“Next Wednesday,” she says. “How you can say anything about him at all, if he’s that far off. Bring adjectives.”
“How many?”
“If he’s infinite?” She caps the last highlighter. “Bring a truck. And Thursday, the tide graph. In ink. I’m not doing your subtraction twice.”

She packs the binder and the highlighters into a canvas bag that has been to a great many beaches, and gets up, and lifts the single-fin out of the rack by the back door, and the barista stops steaming milk to watch the rack go empty again. Skye goes out the back, through the door propped open on a cinder block onto the bike path, with the board under her arm and the towel over her shoulder, barefoot on the warm concrete, and turns toward the water, and doesn’t look back.

The barista comes over with a rag and wipes up the ring of seawater where the binder was. “Same time next week?” she says, to Jack. She looks at the empty slot in the rack. “She paid for the towels. All three. She tipped like it was a bar.”
“Yes,” he says.

He opens his own copy to thirty-nine. The stranger with the pencil quit back at thirty, at the *yes*; this far in, the margins are his. He writes *adjectives* at the top of the page, and under it, after a minute, a question mark. The coffee’s gone cold, and the sand is drying to nothing on the concrete under her chair, and he’s already arguing thirty-nine with her in his head, a week early, and glad, all the way down, that it’s a long book.

s08.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE SECOND-FLOOR KITCHEN — KEEP OUT
body: The second-floor corridor smells of fig and orange peel and hot oil from the stairwell door on, and the smell gets stronger toward the kitchen, whose door stands half shut with a sheet of printer paper taped to it at eye level.

body.title: On the second-floor kitchen door
body.text: KEEP OUT. THIS MEANS YOU, JACK COSTIGAN. EVERYBODY ELSE: KNOCK AND BE SWORN TO SECRECY.

body: Inside, over a sound of frying, Laney is humming something with a key change in it. Jack knocks on the frame under the sign; it seems the least he can do. The door opens a foot and Lena is in the gap: flour to the elbows, a smear of it along one cheekbone, a quilted oven mitt on her left hand with a red lobster on it. She stands so that the gap is exactly as wide as she is. Her hair is tied up in a dish towel, and there’s flour in the towel too.
“You can’t come in.”
“I know. It says.”

“It says *you*, specifically. Laney wanted it in red. I talked her down to black.” She looks at the Catechism under his arm, and back at him, and the fig and the hot oil come out round her into the corridor. “Is it after?”
“It’s after.”

body.text: He tells her the funny part first. The two surfers who asked Skye about the swell like she was the harbor patrol, and nodded at her answer like it settled a bet. The barista with a second towel nobody had asked for, and then a third. “She said it was the only green she owns. For St. Patrick’s.” The corner of Lena’s mouth goes, a very little, and comes back. The rest of it after that, because the rest is why he’s standing at this door: that Skye came in straight out of the water; that she was in a wetsuit peeled down to her waist and tied there by the arms; that above it she had on a bikini top — at which Lena looks past him down the corridor to the fire door, and back; and that they argued thirty-one to thirty-eight for an hour and a half, whether you can get to God from the ocean or from the inside of your own head, and whether you can get anywhere at all without being told.

That Skye came in straight out of the water, in a wetsuit peeled down to her waist and tied there by the arms, and above it a bikini top, green — “the only green she owns,” she said, “for St. Patrick’s.” The two surfers who talked swell with her like she was one of them. The barista’s second towel. That they argued thirty-one to thirty-eight for an hour and a half, whether you can get to God from the ocean or from the inside of your own head, and whether you can get anywhere at all without being told.

body.text: “A draw.”
“I took it.”
“She took it. Fair.”

body: “She kept her hands to herself.”
Lena is quiet for as long as it takes whatever is in the oil behind her to need turning. Inside, Laney turns it, and goes on humming.
“Thank you for telling me.”
She says it beautifully, the way she’d thank a priest at the church door for a homily she means to argue with on the walk home, and he would rather she had thrown the oven mitt at him.
She takes the oven mitt off. She puts it back on. The lobster looks at him.
“Was she good?”
“Yes.”
“Good.” Sharp, and quiet.

choices.text: “You went polite on me.”
choices.key: When you told Lena about Skye’s second Wednesday and she went polite on you, you told her so, and she came back.
response: “You went polite on me.”
“I did.” She doesn’t pretend otherwise; she breathes in through her nose, flour and all. “Give me a second to come back from it.”

She takes the second. He watches her take it, her eyes on the floor tile between his boots and her socks, and then her chin comes up. “There. I’m back.” She leans out through the gap and kisses him, deliberately, with the oven mitt still on and held out to one side so it won’t get flour on the Carhartt.
She goes back in with the mitt raised over her shoulder like a salute.

choices.text: “It’s Wednesday. That’s all it is.”
choices.key: When you told Lena about Skye’s second Wednesday, you told her it was only Wednesday, and she said she knew.
response: “It’s Wednesday. That’s all it is.”
“I know what it is.” Quiet, not sharp. She looks down at the lobster. And again, softer: “I know what it is, Jack.”
She stays in the gap with the mitt on and doesn’t say anything else. She looks at him, and he can see that she’s all right.

choices.text: *Wait. Let her come back on her own.*
choices.key: When you told Lena about Skye’s second Wednesday, you waited until she came back on her own.
response: He waits. The frying fills it.
The mitt comes off. Goes back on. She looks up.
“Friday is still mine.”
The door closes. Jack stands alone in the corridor under his own name in black Sharpie, and on the other side of it Laney takes the key change again.
