body: The rota is still up on the door of 420, at eye level, with enough Scotch tape on it to ride out a hurricane.

body.title: On the door of 420, in three colors of Sharpie
body.text: KEVIN’S CASSEROLE ROTA — THROUGH EASTER. MON: LANEY (KING RANCH CHICKEN). TUE: MARGOT (LENTIL, WITH FOOTNOTES). WED: PETER H. THU: PRIYA. FRI: SPOKEN FOR. SAT: LANEY AGAIN. SUN: CHURCH, THEN LANEY. NO SUBSTITUTIONS. NO REFUSALS. —L.P.

body: Jack knocks.
“It’s open,” Kevin says. “Unfortunately.”

Doug has gone down to the bars on Las Olas in a foam hat shaped like a pint glass, and his half of the room is an unmade bed and an Xbox. Kevin is at his desk in his quarter-zip, under the poster of the human muscular system, eating casserole cold out of a Pyrex dish. The mini-fridge stands open beside him, and in it, stacked like sandbags, there are three more.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, without getting up, “this is what I was afraid of.”

He points his fork at the fridge, top shelf to bottom. “Tuesday. Margot. Lentil, delivered this morning, retroactively. It came with a bibliography. Wednesday. Peter Haddad. Something with tater tots on top that I believe is a Minnesota thing. And that one’s not on the rota. That one’s a *supplement*. Laney left it outside the door at one o’clock this morning with a note that said *in case*. In case of what, she didn’t specify.” He taps the dish in front of him. “Monday. Laney. King Ranch chicken. Also retroactive.”

body.text: “Before the supplement there was a pie. A whole coconut cream, string tied twice, outside the door at midnight. Doug ate a third of it out of the box with his hands before anybody could tell him what it was for.”

body: He holds up a forkful and looks at it with professional interest. “King Ranch chicken is a delivery system for cream of mushroom soup. The sodium in this dish alone is a cardiac event. I’m going to be the first pre-med in the history of Marisol to be hospitalized by kindness.”
“How’d she find out?”

“A soprano.” Kevin says it the way he’d say *a tick*. “On the lagoon steps, last night. One verse and Laney had the names, the date and the reason. I opened my door at seven this morning to go to lab and there was a rota on it and Laney standing next to it. She read it to me. In the hall. With feeling. Like a proclamation from a balcony.” He chews. “Doug won’t touch any of it. Doug says casseroles are for funerals.”
“What’d you tell him?”
“I told him I’m aware of what they’re for.”

He pulls Margot’s lentil out of the fridge and peels back the foil, and there is in fact an index card taped to the inside of it, typed. He reads it aloud in the voice he uses for case studies. “Footnote three. *The lentil is among the oldest cultivated legumes. See Genesis 25, in which a man sells his birthright for a bowl of them. Do not do this.*” He puts the foil back. “Priya’s is tomorrow. She’s laminated the reheating instructions. I’ve seen a draft.”
He fishes a second fork out of the desk drawer and holds it out over his shoulder. Jack pulls Doug’s desk chair over and eats. It’s cold, and good, and there is far too much of it.
Down the hall somebody runs past singing about Galway, badly, and a door bangs on it.
“She said I’m never in the room,” Kevin says. He scrapes a corner of the dish clean. “I’m in this room. I’m in it a lot, actually.”
He eats a tater tot off Peter Haddad’s casserole, cold, out of the fridge, with his fingers.

choices.text: *Rank the casseroles.*
response: Jack ranks them, with tasting notes: the tater tots first, for nerve; Margot’s lentil second, for scholarship; the King Ranch last, for the mushrooms. Kevin disputes every placing on clinical grounds, the tots as a lipid profile and the lentils as a fiber event, and in the end he takes a purple Sharpie out of the cup on his desk, opens the door, and writes the final standings on Laney’s rota under SUN, in a fourth color.

choices.text: “Laney loves you. She’s just bad at it in a good way.”
response: “Laney loves you. She’s just bad at it in a good way.”
“I know.” Kevin looks at the open fridge, at the three dishes under their foil. “It’s the best thing anybody’s done for me all year, and if you tell her I said so I’ll deny it under oath.”
He goes back to eating.

choices.text: “I didn’t tell her.”
response: “I didn’t tell her.”
“I know you didn’t.” Kevin pushes the Pyrex to the middle of the desk. “That’s why I let you in.”
They eat out of the one dish, a fork each, while somebody down the hall puts the Galway song on again.

s09t.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:30 PM · THE SIGMA RHO HOUSE ON THE BLUFF — SHIPPING UP
s09t.music: Dropkick Murphys — “I’m Shipping Up to Boston”
body: The Sigma Rho house sits on the bluff with its back to the Pacific and its deck hung out over the dark like a diving board, and every speaker the brothers own is out on the deck playing the same song, for the third time since Jack came up the side stairs. It’s shoulder to shoulder in green out there: green beads, green plastic bowlers, a boy in a kilt who is not Scottish and a girl explaining to him at length that he’s wearing it wrong. The keg by the rail is putting out something the color of antifreeze. Somewhere indoors, under the speakers, there really is a fiddle, played by a sophomore from Bakersfield who learned it for tonight and is losing.

Theo is at the far end of the rail, alone in the crowd the way he can manage to be, in a blazer of green velvet so deep it looks wet, holding a pint of the green beer he hasn’t touched. When he sees Jack he lifts it, by way of introduction. “Behold. I said velvet. I don’t lie about fabric.”
“You look like a pool table.”

“I look like a pool table in a *Visconti* picture.” He takes a second pint off the rail, where it’s been waiting, and puts it in Jack’s hand. “Say it. You’ve got the face. I could see it from the stairs.”

body.text: So Jack tells him, at the rail, with the water going on in the dark below. That Skye came back to Oceanography two weeks ago. That last Tuesday she put a paperback Catechism down on his notebook and said she wanted to read it with him, from the beginning, in order, one section at a time, until one of them talked the other one round. Wednesdays at four, at Low Tide on Las Olas. That last week she came in a gown, and today she came straight out of the ocean. Theo’s eyebrows go up at *came back*, and they’re still up at *Catechism*. He has turned round to listen, with his back to the party.
body.else: So Jack tells him how the second one went, at the rail, with the water going on in the dark below: straight out of the ocean this time, a wetsuit, thirty-one to thirty-eight.

body.text: “The *whole* thing?”
body.else: “Who won?” Theo says, and Jack tells him, and Theo nods at the dark water for a while.

body.text: “Two thousand eight hundred and sixty-five paragraphs.”
body.else: “She’s going to finish it, you know,” he says. “All of it. She doesn’t know how not to.”

body.text: Theo shuts his eyes. “A girl. A book. Twenty-eight hundred paragraphs and a wetsuit. At Low Tide, which makes a cortado I still think about.” He opens them. “Cannes. Out of competition. They’d have to hose down the Croisette.” Then the pitch goes out of him, and he looks down into his beer. “She finishes things,” he says. “When she was fourteen a director told her she didn’t understand her own character, and she went home and read all of Stanislavski in a weekend so she could tell him why he was wrong. All of it. Came in on the Monday and did. She won.” He turns the pint on the rail. “Other people get bored. She gets to the end. And next week she’ll come in something else. She never wears the same thing twice in front of the same audience. She didn’t when we were eleven.”
A boy in a shamrock bodysuit goes past them singing a different song from the one that’s playing. Theo waits for him to be gone.
“Be careful with her, Costigan,” he says. “Not for you.”

body: “Does Lena know?”
“First, today. Before you.”
“What did she say?”
“‘Thank you for telling me.’”
Theo winces all the way down into the velvet. “Oh, no. The *polite* one.”
“She came back from it.”
“Excellent.” Theo drinks none of his beer, in celebration.
“Friday,” Theo says. “Nineteen.” He shakes his head at the Pacific. “I’ve been nineteen since November. I don’t recommend it. Everybody expects you to have learned something.”

choices.text: *Drink the green beer. One. For St. Patrick, who got rid of the snakes.*
response: He drinks it. It’s terrible: cold, thin, and faintly minty for reasons of its own. Theo watches him get to the bottom like a man watching a nature documentary about something with too many legs.
“Patrick didn’t get rid of the snakes, Costigan. There were never any snakes in Ireland.”
“Then he did a great job.”
Theo laughs, short, into the velvet.

choices.text: *Hold it till it goes flat.*
response: They stand at the rail with two full pints going flat in the wind off the water and talk about nothing much: the boy in the kilt, the Croisette, whether Fenner owns a second cardigan. When the beer is dead Theo takes Jack’s glass out of his hand and pours them both over the rail into the ice plant, one and then the other, with ceremony.

choices.text: “I’m glad it’s you in the other bed, Theo.”
response: “I’m glad it’s you in the other bed, Theo.”
Theo looks at the water. “Don’t. I’ll cry on the velvet, and it doesn’t come out.”
“Me too,” he says, short, still looking at the water.

s10.slug: THURSDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — MISS BROUSSARD TEACHES
body: At ten past two last night the light was still on under the kitchen door on two. He knows because he was on the stairs at ten past two, and the hot oil came up the stairwell to meet him, and he went on up past the landing with his hand on the rail and didn’t knock; the sign on that door has his name on it.

The rain that came through at dawn has left the windows of 302 beaded and the quad below them shining, and somebody has opened the middle one a hand’s width, so the room is cool and the radiator has nothing to argue with. In Morro this morning Skye said *hi* across Pair 41 and then took notes on the tides in green ink for seventy-five minutes, and that was all of her. Fenner did not follow up twice.

Hale has taken Lena’s chair at the window end, as threatened. He sits in it with his legs crossed and *Brideshead* shut on his knee and the fountain pen uncapped and nothing to write on, and Lena stands at the window behind his shoulder with her book open on one palm, so that to see her he has to turn round in his own seat. He keeps turning round.

Her sleeves are shoved to the elbows. At a podium that means she’s about to take somebody apart; here, with a paperback on her palm and the rain light coming off the quad onto one side of her face, it seems to mean only that she is having the time of her life and would rather die than say so.

She’s very good. Jack has watched her take a floor and take this table, every Monday and Thursday since January, and this is neither one: she isn’t arguing, she’s asking. She asks the table things she doesn’t know the answer to, and waits, and lets the sophomores be wrong without rescuing them, and when somebody is right she says so and moves on before they can enjoy it. It is the least Hale-like hour anybody has ever spent in Hollis 302, and Hale, three feet from it, can’t stop turning round to watch.

“Sebastian tells Charles he believes in the star and the three kings,” she says, “because it’s a lovely idea. And Charles says you can’t believe a thing because it’s lovely. And Sebastian says, but I do, that’s how I believe.” She looks down the oak. “Is that a bad reason? I don’t know. I’ve been trying to decide since Sunday.”
Hale twists in the chair. “You don’t *know*?”
“No, Professor. That’s why I asked the table.” She turns a page. “You can tell me afterward, if you’re sure.”

The nose ring says it’s the worst reason there is; it’s how people end up believing in horoscopes. The sophomore beside her says it’s the only reason anybody believes anything, they just dress it up afterward in footnotes. Yusuf says his grandmother believes in the evil eye because it’s a *terrible* idea, and asks whether that’s better or worse, and nobody knows, and Lena points her pencil at him like he’s won a raffle. When the nose ring tells her flatly that she’s wrong about Julia, Hale turns round the other way in his chair to look at the nose ring, only look, and the nose ring withdraws the remark. Caleb has his pen capped on his book again, and Lena leaves him be.
“Sebastian isn’t a fool,” Lena says. “He’s the only person at Oxford who suspects a lovely idea might be lovely because it’s true. And he’s terrified of what it’ll cost him if —”
“Yes,” Hale says.
She stops.
“Yes. That is the book. Go on.”
He has interrupted every person at this table since January, most of them inside their first clause, and never yet to agree with one. Two of the sophomores look at each other. Lena goes on.

She takes them through the end of Book One: the summer over, Charles going back up to Oxford, Sebastian drinking alone in his rooms and lying about it, the happiness already being buried somewhere for later. “It’s a love story,” she says. “Whatever else it is. Book One is a love story.”
Hale doesn’t turn round this time. “Miss Broussard, everything is a love story to someone who’s just won something.”

The table laughs, the sophomores loudest; at the door end Jack keeps his face exactly where it was. Lena looks at nobody — not Hale, not the door end, a knot in the oak halfway down — and when the laugh has run out she turns a page and goes on as if he’d remarked on the rain.
With ten minutes left she looks down the length of the table to the door end, to him.
“Why does Sebastian need the bear?”

choices.text: “Because it can’t leave.”
response: Lena turns to the table with it. “Mr. Costigan says because it can’t leave.”
Down the side of the oak Caleb looks up from his capped pen, at Jack, and down again. By then Lena is already asking the nose ring whether Charles can.

choices.text: “Because Charles might.”
response: “Mr. Costigan has peeked,” Hale says, before she can.
“Mr. Costigan has read the *back cover*.”
The table enjoys it, Hale most of all. Lena turns a page and doesn’t look at the door end, and the corner of her mouth is doing something she will not let it finish.

choices.text: “Because it’s the only thing at Oxford he doesn’t have to explain himself to.”
response: She doesn’t give that one to the table. She looks at him across the oak until Yusuf coughs, and then turns to Yusuf and asks him about Julia.
At her elbow Hale opens his *Brideshead* and writes in it. Lena stands at the window with her back to the room for the length of Yusuf’s answer, looking out at the wet quad.

s10a.slug: THURSDAY · 4:10 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT DESK — FAVE
body: Marcus is on the front desk with his hood up and his orgo open in front of him to a page of hexagons, and on the shelf behind him, between a Zappos box and somebody’s red Netflix envelope, there is a shoebox wrapped in a Giant Eagle grocery bag and taped round and round like a crime scene. Jack would know the hand on it in the dark. It has been on every Easter envelope he ever got, with a five-dollar bill folded in quarters inside and a holy card on top of the five so he’d see the saint first.

body.title: A shoebox in a Giant Eagle bag, Priority Mail
body.text: MISS LENA BROUSSARD · DELGATO HALL · ROOM 217 · from C. RINALDI, GLENWOOD AVE., YOUNGSTOWN, OHIO

body: Nonna’s capitals go uphill and come down hard, every letter a fence post driven in by somebody who learned to write from nuns with rulers and has never seen the point of joining anything up. Priority Mail, Monday’s postmark, from the post office on Glenwood where she still goes in person to buy one stamp at a time.
“That’s my grandmother,” Jack says.
Marcus looks at the box, and at him. “It says Broussard, man.”
“It’s my grandmother’s handwriting.”

“It’s Broussard’s box.” He lifts it off the shelf to show Jack the name, as a courtesy, and it rattles: a dry, small, many-voiced sound, a maraca somebody was too polite to shake. Beans. A shoebox of dried beans, from Ohio. “I buzzed 217 when it came,” Marcus says. “Twenty minutes ago.” He puts it back on the shelf and sits down in front of it.
“I could sign for it.”
“You could sign for your *own* stuff.”

The stairwell door bangs open. Lena comes across the lobby at a dead run in her socks, her hair coming down out of its pencil, and reaches past Marcus’s head and takes the box off the shelf, and puts it behind her back with both hands.
“You didn’t see this.”
“It’s from my grandmother.”
“It’s from *Nonna*,” she says. “That’s a different thing.”
She backs away to the stairwell with the box behind her, rattling at every step, and goes up two at a time.
Marcus watches the door until it stops moving. He turns a page of hexagons. “Your grandma spells it with a T.”
Jack laughs, alone in the middle of the lobby with his bag still on his shoulder, and can’t stop, and Marcus waits him out with the patience of a man who is paid by the hour.

s11.slug: THURSDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE CROSS CAN WAIT
body: The sun is down behind the hills but the sky hasn’t heard yet, and the doors of St. Brendan’s are propped open on the last of the light. On the left-hand door, under the Mass times, there’s a sheet of paper in Father Osei’s slow upright hand.

body.title: Taped to the door of St. Brendan’s
body.text: STATIONS TONIGHT (THURSDAY). TOMORROW IS A SOLEMNITY. —G.O.

body: Inside, the forty are the forty, on the wrong night: the old man with his own kneeling pad, the three nursing students still in scrubs from a late lab, the Knights in their windbreakers, the woman who sits by the third station all evening so she won’t have to walk to it. Lena is already in his pew when he gets there, lace on, booklet open on her palm. When he sits he sees flour in the crease of one knuckle, and when she turns a page there is anise on the air between the pews, faint, under the candle wax. Her eyes have the look they get at the end of a double at the Anchor. He doesn’t ask.
Father Osei comes down the aisle behind the cross in the purple stole and goes up to the ambo before the first station, and looks out at them over the book.
“Tomorrow is St. Joseph,” he says. “The cross will wait one day; it is used to waiting.”
A laugh goes along the pews, low, the kind a church allows itself. Five Fridays in, and this one on a Thursday.

It throws everybody a little. The old man with the kneeling pad starts toward the first station before Gus has given the chord, and stops, and looks up at the loft for permission. One of the nursing students has brought a Friday’s worth of Kleenex. Jack’s knees know this tile by now; they don’t know it on a Thursday, and they tell him so at the first station and the second.

Gus gives the chord from the loft and they go down the south wall and up the north, singing between the carvings, *Let me mingle tears with thee, / mourning him who mourned for me*, the forty a little behind the organ and Lena a little ahead of the forty. Her lips go a half-beat before the responses at every station. She knows them better than the book does.

The thirteenth is near the back, where the light from the doors doesn’t reach. *Jesus is taken down from the cross.* Two men on ladders in the carving, and a sheet, and the body coming down into his mother’s lap as if she had held out her arms for a parcel and been handed this. Father Osei reads it short, his eyes on the page: that they took him down, and gave him to her, and she held what they gave her. Then the church kneels.

Jack kneels on it. *Keep her*, he says, without saying who, and it’s Ma at the sink on Glenwood, and it’s the lace a foot from his shoulder, and he doesn’t sort out which, and the forty stand him back up.

Afterward the steps are cool and the town below has its lights on. Over the hills behind the olive tree a crescent moon is going down, thin as a bead of solder. People come out past them doing up their jackets. She comes down two steps ahead of him and turns round.

Father Osei is at the door behind them, taking hands, being told by the old man with the kneeling pad that Thursday felt wrong. When it’s Jack’s turn he holds on to the hand a little and says, “Tomorrow, Jack, wear a clean shirt.”
Beside Jack, Lena says, “*Father*.”
“It is only advice about shirts,” Father Osei says, and gives his hand to the next person, delighted with himself.
“Go to bed, Costigan,” Lena says. “I’ve got bread.”
She goes down Ocean Road toward the harbor at a walk that wants to be a run, and twice it nearly is, and twice she reins it in.

He sits down on the top step. At the bottom of the hill the Anchor is lit as it always is, the neon anchor and the booths along the window and Gloria’s counter; and then one more light comes on, a small square at the back by Rudy’s ovens, the window that is dark every night he has ever worked a shift. He stays where he is with his elbows on his knees, the crescent going down by degrees over the ridge, and watches that one window.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 12:01 AM · DELGADO HALL, HIS STEP — NINETEEN
body: The tube light over the fourth-floor door has the stairwell to itself. Jack is on his step, third down from four, in the Carhartt over a T-shirt and his socks, with the RAZR open on his knee and its little screen the brightest thing on the concrete. He came out at half past eleven for no reason he could have given Theo, and has been watching the minutes go over ever since like a kid watching the odometer on the Turnpike, waiting for all the nines.
The stairwell carries on as before. The light buzzes. He’s nineteen, and it feels a great deal like eighteen with the lights off, and he is thinking about getting up.

He has been told not to see a good many things this week. He has laid none of them end to end, on purpose, as you’d leave a present on the table and walk around it, and he isn’t going to start at midnight on a stairwell.

The screen has just gone over to 12:01 when feet come up from two, fast, slapping the concrete, taking the turn at the landing on one hand. Lena comes round the corner breathing hard from the hill: flour in her hair, flour on the knees of her jeans, the Saints sweatshirt with a brown scorch on one cuff in the shape of an oven rack, and on her hands, when she gets close, anise, and sugar, and the hot metal of the inside of an oven. She stops a step below him, so that she has to look up.
“It’s the nineteenth,” she says.
He looks at her — the flour, the scorch, the knot of hair she must have put up at seven and given up on by ten, the hill still going in and out of her — and can’t think of one smart thing to say.

She takes his face in both her floury hands and kisses him, quick, the way you’d stamp a thing to say it’s been seen to — and then not quick at all. She tastes of sugar and anise, and her cheek is cold from Ocean Road, and her mouth isn’t. He has the RAZR in one hand and nothing in the other and puts the empty one on the back of her sweatshirt, where it’s warm from running, and she leans up into him off the lower step, and the first kiss at nineteen goes on long enough that the light over the door has time to flicker twice.
She ends it. Her thumbs stay on his cheekbones a second.
“You ran up the hill,” he says.
“I ran up the hill. Rudy timed me. He’s going to tell everybody eleven minutes. It was nine.” She’s still getting her breath. “I wanted to be first.”
“First what?”
“First anybody.”
“You burned your sweatshirt.”

She looks at the cuff as if it were somebody else’s. “The back of that oven runs hot. Everybody told me. I didn’t listen to everybody.” She looks down the stairwell. “I have *dough* proofing on top of Rudy’s ovens.”

Ocean Road is a mile of hill each way. She ran up it for one minute on his stairs, and she is going to run back down it, at midnight, to bread he isn’t allowed to see. One foot is already on the step below.

body: He has been awake since six with nowhere to be till noon, and couldn’t go back, and has come down to her landing in his socks as he does, and her step is empty; the window over it is going from navy to the color of the inside of a shell, and down Ocean Road, he’d bet his tips, Rudy’s fryer has been on since five. He sits on her step anyway. When the RAZR goes the screen says GLENWOOD and 6:41, and he knows before he has it open: 9:41 Eastern, the minute he was born. Ma has called at it every year of his life, wherever he was — last year in the hall outside Latin at Mooney, with the second declension coming through the door — and he had forgotten she would.
“Seven pounds, eleven ounces,” Ma says, instead of hello. “Your father makes me say it. Happy birthday, sweetheart.”
“Hi, Ma.”

“Nineteen. I don’t know how that happened. I was there for all of it and I don’t know how.” A breath, Glenwood’s kitchen in it, the radio going on the windowsill. “I took the morning. Don’t tell anybody at St. Brigid’s I took it for this, they think I’m at the dentist.”

body: He opens his mouth.
“I’m not telling you what about. She’d kill me. I like her.”
“What did she —”
“What are you doing today?” Ma says, right over him.
“Mass at noon. I don’t know after that. Lena said —”

“Don’t tell me. I’m not supposed to know anything. I’m a school secretary, I know everything in that building and nothing in this one.” And, in the same breath: “Rosie mailed you something. I wasn’t allowed to see it. It went in an envelope with four stamps on it because she didn’t trust three.”

There is a click on the line, the extension in the front room coming off its hook, and breathing, and then Nonna, from Glenwood and eighty-four years away, loud, the way she talks to telephones: “*Auguri, Giacomino.*” And then something longer, fast, in the Calabrese he grew up under the table hearing and never learned, and in the middle of it he catches *fave* and nothing else.

“She says the girl has the beans,” Ma says. “She says that’s all she’ll say on a telephone.” Away from the receiver: “*Sì, Mà*, he heard you. The street heard you.” And to him, lower: “She’s been good this week. She’s had the calendar out on the table since Sunday. She knew what Friday was before I did.”

And Ma, quick and bright, the way she reads the lunch menu over the PA at St. Brigid’s: “When you were little Nonna did the table in the dining room. Danny was always Joseph. You were too little to be anything but the Bambino. You used to cry when they put you in the laundry basket.” And straight on, without a stop: “Is it nice out there? It’s pouring. Your father’s out on the porch watching it come down like it owes him money.”
“It’s nice,” Jack says. Over the landing the window has gone white with the morning.

A girl from three comes down past him in shower shoes with her caddy under her arm, and he pulls his knees in to let her by, and she mouths *sorry*, and he mouths *happy birthday* back at her by mistake, and she goes on down looking puzzled and pleased.
The RAZR buzzes against his ear while she’s telling him about the rain. He takes it away and looks.

body: At ten past twelve St. Brendan’s is white. Four weeks of purple and bare wood, and today Father Osei comes up the aisle in white and gold, and there are lilies on the flower stands either side of the altar where for a month there has been nothing but the stands, and the noon crowd — office people on their lunch hour, nursing students, two Knights, the woman with the walker, the Newman regulars in a clump near the front — looks up at it all like people who walked into the wrong church and are glad of it.

He has a clean shirt on under the Carhartt, the white one, ironed on Theo’s board. Lena is beside him in white lace. It’s her grandmother’s other veil, the one for feasts, and it makes her look like somebody he hasn’t met yet and would like to.

Up in the loft Gus, who has had four weeks of keeping it in, lets the Gloria out like a held breath — *Gloria in excelsis Deo* — the first since Ash Wednesday, and the noon crowd that doesn’t know the words sings anyway, and Lena beside him knows every one of them and sings them with her chin up, and Jack sings badly and doesn’t care who hears.

Father Osei reads Matthew. Joseph, a righteous man, finding her with child, and unwilling to expose her to shame; deciding to do it quietly; going to sleep on it; the angel in the dream — *do not be afraid* — and Joseph waking up and doing what he was told. That’s all Matthew gives him: no lines. He wakes up, and gets up, and does it. Jack has known men built that way, on the line at Lordstown and down the end of the bar at the K of C, and has always assumed they had nothing to say.

Father Osei closes the book and gives them two sentences. “Matthew calls Joseph a righteous man, and then tells us the righteous thing he had planned was to be quiet, and kind, and let nobody throw anything at her. Before any angel came, he had already decided that much on his own.”

They say the Creed, which nobody has said on a Friday since New Year’s Day, and the noon crowd stumbles into it. At *by the power of the Holy Spirit* Lena bows, and has hold of his elbow, and doesn’t seem to know she’s got it.

Afterward, in the courtyard, under the olive tree, the noon people go off to their cars and the sprinkler comes on over by the fence and somebody runs to turn it off. Lena takes the veil off and folds it. Father Osei goes by them toward the rectory with his vestments over his arm, looks once at Jack’s collar, says, “Clean shirt,” with satisfaction, and keeps going.
He opens the RAZR to the three texts and holds it out to her.
She reads them. All three, and his.
“That was kind of her.”
She closes the phone against her palm, carefully, so the cracked hinge won’t catch, and puts it back into his hand, and keeps her fingers on it a moment before she lets go.

body.text: She turns to her bag. “No fast today. It’s a solemnity. Canon twelve fifty-one. I checked it twice and I asked a priest.” He had been going to keep bread and water till sundown. She has taken that off him like a coat at the door.
body.else: She turns to her bag. “You don’t have to eat fish today. It’s a solemnity. Canon twelve fifty-one. I checked it twice and I asked a priest.” He had been going to have the fish sticks at the Commons. She has taken that off him like a coat at the door.

body: “Which priest?”
“Father Osei. He laughed at me for a full minute, and then he said yes, and then he said I could have looked it up, and I said I *had*, twice.”

Out of the bag she brings a white bakery box tied with string, and out of the box, on a square of wax paper, a zeppola: a ring of fried dough, gold, split and piped full of cream, with a candied cherry sunk in the middle like a stone in a ring.
“Nonna’s recipe,” she says. “Rudy’s fryer. Five o’clock this morning. Rudy said the oil was too hot.” She lifts her chin. “Rudy was wrong.”
“You had one?”
“I ate the ugly ones at six. It’s a solemnity.”

He eats it standing under the olive tree at noon on a Friday in Lent. It is soft still at the center, and the cream is cold from Rudy’s walk-in and has lemon peel in it, grated so fine you don’t see it, only taste it, and he knows on the first bite whose kitchen that came out of, and has to stop chewing a minute. She watches him eat it with her arms folded. “Is it right?” she says. “Tell me the truth. If the cream’s wrong I can go back down.” He can’t answer her with his mouth full, and then he can’t answer her for a different reason, and he nods instead, twice, and she looks down into the empty bakery box and says, “Good,” very quietly, to the box. Sugar comes off it down the front of the Carhartt, and she brushes it away with the back of her hand, brisk, as her mother would brush down a child on the church steps. He eats the cherry last.
Lena takes the empty wax paper out of his hand and folds it into the box and the box into her bag, and walks backward three steps toward the gate.
“Five-thirty. The Fishbowl. Bring everybody you’ve ever met.”

s15.slug: FRIDAY · 5:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — A TABLE FOR A SAINT
body: The sun is low enough now to come straight down the lobby from the west doors, and the Fishbowl has gone gold in it, all four glass walls, so that from the mailboxes Jack can see the light in the room before he can see into it. Somebody has taped butcher paper across the lower half of the glass on the lobby side. It stops at about chin height. Over the top of it a row of heads he knows turns toward him at once, and Laney’s hand comes up and pulls Doug Pruitt’s head down out of sight, too late, and then her own.

Lena is outside the door, on the lobby side, with her back to the butcher paper. She’s in a blue dress with small white buttons he has never seen before, and an apron over it she has forgotten to take off, and her grandmother’s medal, and there is still a dusting of flour in the crook of one elbow. She looks him over once — the Carhartt, the flannel, the jeans he washes dishes in — and nods, a woman checking an item off a list.

body.text: She puts her hand on the push bar and doesn’t push it yet. “You’re going to cry,” she says. “I want you to.” She leans on the bar.
body.else: She puts her hand on the push bar and leans on it without a word.

body: The noise comes out at him — Laney’s “*Surprise!*” a little late, because everybody was waiting for somebody else to start; a whoop from Theo; Margot saying “Happy birthday” at an ordinary speaking volume — and under it Louis Prima, out of Theo’s iPhone, which is standing in a coffee mug on a side table for a speaker, so that the song comes out of the mug sounding like it’s being sung up from the bottom of a well in Naples. The couches have been shoved back against the windows. The broken foosball table is up against the wall under a bedsheet, and there is something rectangular under the sheet that nobody is looking at. He knows two-thirds of the people in here and has been introduced to the rest.

He doesn’t want a fuss. Everybody in this room knows it; it’s possible that’s why there are so many of them. He stands just inside the door with his hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and takes them out again, because Nonna would have them off at the wrist, and nods at people with his father’s wake nod, chin down and up. Kevin lifts a paper plate at him. Peter Haddad, who drove the Newman van to San Francisco and has never let anybody forget it, is filming on a Canon the size of a deck of cards. He says, “You guys,” which is not a sentence, and Lena, behind him, puts two fingers in the small of his back and steers him in.

The altar is against the long wall where the TV usually lives, and it goes up in three steps nearly to the ceiling tiles. There are milk crates under it — he can see a blue one where a cloth doesn’t quite reach the carpet — and across the top tier a door, a real door, six panels and the hole for the knob, off its hinges from somewhere in the basement. Three white tablecloths over everything, three slightly different whites. “One from every dining hall on this campus,” Laney announces to the room, “and every one goes back Monday morning, so if you spill, you are dead to me.”
“Three tiers,” Lena is telling an RA with a lanyard, “one for each Person of the Trinity. And the saint goes at the top, where he’d be most embarrassed.”

body.text: At the top, between two votives in red glass, in a brass frame he has never seen, is a holy card with its corners worn soft as cloth: Saint Joseph with the lilies and the Child and the carpenter’s square, *PRIEZ POUR NOUS*. He knows it before he’s halfway across the room. It lives on the ledge over his bed in 412, propped against the wall by his alarm clock, and he hasn’t looked at the ledge since Thursday. Across the room Theo is adjusting the coffee mug a little to the left, very precisely.
body.else: At the top, between two votives in red glass, in a brass frame he has never seen, is a holy card from the rack on the Newman table: Saint Joseph with the lilies and the Child and the carpenter’s square, propped up like a portrait over a mantel.

body: There are white lilies on every tier, in Albertsons cellophane with the price stickers turned to the wall. “He gets lilies,” Lena tells the RA. “It’s his whole look.”

The breads are on the middle tier, and he has to stand in front of them and read them, because they are bread and they are also things. A long loaf with dough flowers bunched at the top: the staff. A braid: the beard. Two flat soles with the straps scored in: sandals. A hammer. A cross. Two in the back row came out burned at one end. And in front, dead center, where you would put the thing you were proudest of, there is a loaf in the shape of the state of Ohio.

It is unmistakably Ohio. The lake ragged along the top, the river scalloping the bottom, the two straight sides where Indiana and Pennsylvania begin. Up in the right-hand corner, about where Youngstown is, somebody has pricked one hole with a toothpick. That’s what does it. Not the door off the basement, not the lilies, not the room full of people with plates. A hole the size of a pencil point in a piece of bread, put there by somebody who looked it up.
“That’s Ohio,” Lena tells the floor, not him. “The hole is Youngstown. Rudy wanted to do Cleveland too, and I told him nobody asked for Cleveland.”

He has to look at the fava beans for some time after that. They are in a cut-glass bowl that must belong to the Newman Center, brown and flat and dry, Nonna’s, out of a shoebox from Glenwood Avenue. Beside them, Celeste’s cuccidati in the blue Royal Dansk tin from Dupre Street, with the lid propped against it. Zeppole, Nonna’s kind, the cream piped in and a candied cherry pressed into every one. Lemons and oranges heaped on all three tiers. A dozen stuffed artichokes packed with crumbs and garlic. A foil pan of spaghetti under a drift of toasted breadcrumbs, and Margot, passing behind him with a plate, says, “The breadcrumbs represent sawdust, because he was a carpenter, and I checked three sources and every one of them said so with a straight face,” and keeps going. The lagane e ceci, wide noodles and chickpeas, Nonna’s, carried out here through two telephones. Rudy’s fish, whole and fried gold, on a platter with its mouth open as if it has something to say about the oven.

body.text: And on the bottom tier, among the lemons, a bottle of Barq’s, unopened, standing with its label turned out. He knows that bottle. Lena is explaining the Trinity to a sophomore, and does not look at him while he looks at it.

body: None of it has been within a mile of a cow. “It was a Lenten table before it was a feast,” Lena tells Doug Pruitt, who wanted to know why the fish has a face, “and you don’t change a recipe on a saint.”

On the side table, beside Theo’s coffee mug, there is a stockpot from the Anchor with its lid on, and a ladle laid across a saucer. Lena has stood a folding chair in front of it, like a velvet rope at a museum.

Father Osei comes in from the lobby at a quarter to six with his stole in his coat pocket and a Smucker’s jar of holy water with the label soaked off, and the room gets quieter without anyone deciding to. He kisses the stole and puts it on over his sweater. He blesses in Latin first, the old grace — *Benedic, Domine, nos et haec tua dona* — unhurried, and then in English, in his own words: this table and the hands that made it; the bread and the beans and the fish; the poor who will eat from it tomorrow; all fathers — and there his voice does one small thing, and goes on — and this young man, on his feast. He shakes the water off his fingers over the three tiers, and it patters on the cellophane, and some of it lands on Jack. Jack notices only that he looks at the card at the top a moment longer than he looked at the bread. He wets his fingers again and blesses the bowl of beans by itself.
“The *tupa tupa*!” Laney claps twice, in a voice built for a stadium. “Places. Jack, you’re Joseph, Lena, you’re Mary, y’all go out in the lobby and knock —”
“Absolutely not,” Lena says.

That’s all she says. Laney looks across the altar at Theo, over the lilies, and Theo looks back at her. Theo goes back to the coffee mug and Laney to her clipboard, and as far as Jack can tell he is the only person in the Fishbowl who saw it.

So Margot is Joseph. She has a mop handle out of the second-floor janitor’s closet for a staff, with a lily duct-taped to the top, and she holds it like a halberd. “I’ve done the reading,” she says. Laney is Mary, in the blue shower curtain off the fourth-floor bathroom, worn as a mantle and safety-pinned at the throat: hips back, chin up, a hand at her heart. In the crook of her arm, swaddled in a dish towel, is Coco the coconut, the Bambino for the evening, looking up at the ceiling tiles with a perfectly serene Sharpie face. They process out to the lobby. They knock on the glass.
Theo, inside, an apron over his cashmere and a dish towel on his arm, opens the door a crack. “No room. There’s a convention. Orthodontists.” He shuts it.

Laney knocks again, harder, and Coco nearly goes. Theo opens it another crack. “Still no room. I’ve read this one. A couple, a donkey, no reservation. Every studio in town passed. Nobody is financing a period piece in this economy.” He shuts it.

The third knock comes while Theo has gone back to fix the music. Kevin is standing by the door with an empty plate he hasn’t been allowed to fill, and he opens it, mildly, because somebody is knocking. Laney sails in past him, then turns round and takes him by the elbow too, and steers him to the card table where the saints are to be fed first — Margot, and herself, and Coco in her towel.
“Laney. I opened a door.”
“Because the brokenhearted count, sugar.” She sits him down. And he lets her.

After the saints, everybody, standing, off paper plates. The walls are glass, and people going by in the lobby slow down, and look in, and are waved inside: a kid from Ferrer with a skateboard under his arm, who eats three zeppole one after another and says “Dude” softly to each of them; two RAs; Marcus from the desk, who has put a sign on the desk bell and stands by the window with a plate of fish, having signed for half of this table this week and wanting to see how it came out; a tall girl from the Newman band. Gloria and Rudy are at the end of the table. Gloria has her coat on and something beside her under a dish towel that she has told three separate people not to touch. Rudy is watching people eat his fish, and nods every time somebody takes from the head end.

People keep coming up to say happy birthday, and Jack keeps saying thanks, and at some point it stops being something he has to get through. He eats a zeppola in two bites and gets cream on the Carhartt. He eats an artichoke leaf by leaf, standing by the window with Kevin, who explains the anatomy of an artichoke heart for a test Jack is apparently going to have on it. He is laughing at something Theo has said about the fish when Lena takes him by the sleeve and walks him to the side table, and moves the folding chair, and lifts the lid off the stockpot.

He knows it by the smell before he looks. Escarole, and the broth, and the Parmesan, and under it whatever it is his mother does that nobody else does: the kitchen on Glenwood on any Sunday in winter, with the windows steamed. He looks. The escarole gone dark and soft, the acini di pepe, the meatballs the size of marbles — the size Ma rolls them between her palms, a hundred at a time, with the phone in the crook of her neck.
Meat. On a Friday. In Lent.

He looks at her. Lena Broussard has not eaten meat on a Friday in Lent since she was old enough to be told why. On Dupre Street the altar is meatless and so is the house — shrimp, crawfish, red beans without the ham — and he knows it as well as he knows her handwriting.
“It’s a solemnity,” she says. “The Church says I may.” She lets it stand long enough for him to hear the rest coming. “It doesn’t say I have to.”
She ladles two of the Commons’ waxed-paper coffee cups full, and hands him one, and lifts hers.
“That’s how much I like you, Costigan.”

Then she fishes out a meatball with a plastic spoon and eats it, solemnly, like a woman taking an oath, with her eyes on his — and her face betrays her. It’s good. It’s much too good. She makes a face at it, scandalized, as though the soup has cheated.

choices.text: “It tastes like Glenwood.”
choices.key: At the St. Joseph altar Lena built for your birthday, you tasted your mother’s wedding soup and told her it tasted like home.
response: “Your mother said you’d say that,” Lena says. “She said if you didn’t, I’d used the wrong escarole.”

He drinks, and it isn’t the wrong escarole. It’s Ma’s, down to the pepper she puts in when nobody’s watching. Before he’s finished, Lena takes the cup out of his hand and fills it again from the pot, as she would in her own kitchen for somebody home from school who hasn’t eaten.

She doesn’t make it any bigger than that. She puts her hand on his sleeve, on the canvas at his wrist, in front of Theo and the Ferrer kid and Marcus from the desk and everybody with a paper plate, and only takes it back to pick up her soup.
