She eats another meatball at him, deliberately, holding his eye while she chews, chin up — defiant about it, and delighted about it, and plainly not stopping till the cup is empty.

s16.slug: FRIDAY · 6:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — TRUMBULL
body: The RAZR goes off against his ribs in the middle of a cuccidato. He feels it before he hears it; you couldn’t hear a smoke alarm in the Fishbowl. On the little outside screen, the long 330 number he has never saved and never needed to.

He is out through the lobby and into the east stairwell by the third ring, and up the first half flight, where he sits down on the turn with the concrete cold through his jeans and the party shrinks to Louis Prima and thirty people coming up through the floor. He opens the phone. The recorded woman runs through her paragraph — prepaid, Trumbull Correctional, monitored and recorded — with his brother’s name dropped into the hole in the middle of it in his brother’s own voice. He presses one.
“*Professor.*”

Danny doesn’t wait for hello. He sings. He gets as far as *Happy birthday* in a voice like a garbage disposal with a spoon in it, and somebody on the block behind him yells something that doesn’t make it through the line, and Danny says, off the phone, “It’s my *brother’s* birthday, Reggie, have a little *class*,” and Jack is laughing on the step with his forehead on his knee.
“Nineteen,” Danny says, and coughs. “You feel old?”
“I feel nineteen.”
“That’s the trouble with it.” A television behind him, a game, a whistle, men groaning at a call. “Ma says the veil girl’s doing a table.”
“She did it.”
“She *did* it.” Danny says it slow, like he’s writing it on the wall. “So? What’d she do?”

And Jack tells him, the short version: the three tiers and the door off the basement, the lilies, the bread like Ohio with the hole in it, the fish, Laney marching a coconut out to the lobby to knock on the glass. Danny interrupts once. “There’s a cake?”
“There’s something under a sheet on the foosball table that everybody’s pretending isn’t there.”
“Under a *sheet*. Like a body.” He’s delighted. “Go on.” And when Jack has gone on, to the end, Danny says, “Who played Joseph?”
“Margot.”
“Who’s Margot?”
“You’d like her. She has footnotes.”

Danny laughs. It’s the big one, the one that gets away from him and goes on and turns into the cough at the end, and somebody on his end tells him to keep it down, and he doesn’t. And then, still laughing, lighter than anything: “That was always me. You were the baby.” And straight on, without a breath: “Hey — the C.O. finished it. The book. Took him since October. Still says it’s about a house. I says, it’s about a *family*, Officer, and he says, Costigan, what do you think a house is.”
Jack sits on the step with the phone against his ear, and the line goes past him the way a car goes past a man on a curb.

Reggie, Danny reports, has taken up crochet for the arthritis in his hands and is making Danny a hat in wine and gold whether Danny wants one or not, and measured Danny’s head for it with a shoelace while he was asleep. There’s a new guy on the block from Akron who cries at Cavs games, actual tears, a grown man with a neck tattoo. The Cavs keep winning, and Danny refuses to discuss it in case it hears him. The food is the food. Ma sounded good Wednesday. Pop even got on the phone.
“You smoking?”
“Lent.”
“Good.”

The pack is where it has been since Ash Wednesday, in the breast pocket of the Carhartt: Marlboro Reds, the cellophane still on, day thirty-one. He can smell them through it, or thinks he can. It’s a solemnity. It’s his birthday. There is a priest in the next room who would at least hear the argument out. He puts his hand over the pocket, feels the hard corner of the box through the canvas, and takes the hand away.

Below him the lobby door opens and Lena comes through sideways with a paper plate in each hand, a cuccidato on each, and sees the phone, and stops at the foot of the flight. She doesn’t come any farther.

choices.text: *Hand Lena the phone.*
choices.key: When Danny called from Trumbull on your birthday, you handed Lena the phone so she could tell him about the table.

response.text: He holds it out to her. She sets the plates on the bottom step and comes up to the turn and takes the phone in both hands. “Danny? It’s Lena.” “The veil girl,” Danny says, loud enough that Jack can hear it from where he sits.
response.else: He holds it out to her. She sets the plates on the bottom step and comes up to the turn and takes the phone in both hands. “Hello?” “Who’s this?” Danny says, loud enough that Jack can hear it from where he sits. “Lena.” “*The* Lena.”

response: And she tells him what was on the table — all of it, in order, the way she’d tell a parish what the fish fry cleared: the tiers and why there are three, the staff and the beard and the sandals, the two loaves Rudy’s oven ruined, Ohio, the fish, the beans out of Nonna’s own shoebox, her mother’s fig cookies. At the zeppole Danny stops her. “Nonna’s?” Jack hears him say, small through the speaker. “Nonna’s,” Lena says. “Your mother read them to me over the phone, and Nonna corrected her twice.” There’s a pause from Trumbull, and when it comes it’s Danny to her, not to him: “Thanks for doing it. Somebody ought to.”

The recording breaks in over whatever she was going to say back — one minute — and she gives Jack the phone without a word. He gets ten seconds. “Love you, Professor. Happy birthday.” After that there’s no hallway in his ear anymore, no game, no Reggie: only the stairwell. Lena has gone down for the plates and come back, and is sitting on the step below his with her back against the rail, a paper plate on each knee.

choices.text: “She did the whole thing, D. Nonna’s table. In a dorm.”
choices.key: When Danny called from Trumbull on your birthday, you told him Lena had done Nonna’s whole table, in a dorm.
response: On the line Danny says, “*Good.*”

Nothing, for the length of a free throw, but the game on the television behind him and one long breath going out of him somewhere in Trumbull County. It is the closest Danny comes. A tone cuts in, and the recorded woman, flat as a bus schedule, says there is one minute remaining. “Love you, Professor. Happy birthday.” And the line is simply gone, mid-whistle.
Lena comes up the flight with the plates and sits down beside him on his step, close, and hands him one, and eats her cookie, and looks at the cinderblock wall with him, which tonight is the view.

choices.text: *Keep him to yourself for the fifteen minutes.*
choices.key: When Danny called from Trumbull on your birthday, you kept him to yourself for all fifteen minutes.
response: He lifts one finger to her over the rail. She nods.

So he and Danny talk about nothing. The Cavs, who are not to be discussed. Reggie’s hat. The weather in Leavittsburg: rain, sideways. “God sends it to Trumbull County special, Professor. It ain’t raining anywhere else in Ohio.” Whether Pop has fixed the storm door yet. He hasn’t. Twelve more minutes of nothing at all, and the best twelve of the day. The warning comes in like a hand on his shoulder. “Love you, Professor. Happy birthday.” And then just the stairwell, and the party downstairs.
He looks down. Lena is at the foot of the flight where she has been all along, and when he looks she holds a plate up to him at arm’s length, a cuccidato on it.

s16a.slug: FRIDAY · 7:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — THE LUCKY BEAN
body: The sun has gone behind the hills, and the glass walls have turned to mirrors, so that the Fishbowl looks twice its size and has two altars in it, the real one and its reflection standing out over the dark lawn. The real one is two-thirds gone. Father Osei left at seven with a plate under foil for the rectory and a lemon in each coat pocket. The Ferrer kid is asleep in an armchair with his skateboard on his chest.

Laney whips the sheet off the foosball table. Under it is a Texas sheet cake in a pan nearly as big as the table, chocolate, with pecans all over the top and nineteen candles set in it in what might be the shape of a 19. Lena exiled it there at five o’clock. (“It’s *cake*, Laney, not a sacramental.”) Laney drops a sash over Jack’s head — white satin, rhinestones, BIRTHDAY BOY — and settles it across the Carhartt from shoulder to hip, and steps back to judge it, and the room sings at him in four keys, Margot half a beat behind everybody on purpose. He blows the candles out in two tries, and is given a corner piece, because the birthday boy gets a corner, Laney says; it’s in the Constitution. Lena is by the lilies with her arms folded, singing louder than anyone, and flat.

Then the presents, which he was told there wouldn’t be. From Kevin, a box of medical-grade nitrile gloves, size large, for the Hobart: “For the maceration.” From Theo, a one-sheet of *Rocky* in a black frame: “The most Catholic film ever made, Costigan. The first thing you see is Jesus over the ring, and the whole last reel is a man shouting a girl’s name.” From Margot, an index card, typed, handed over face down. From Gloria, the thing under the dish towel, a coconut cream pie, set into his hands — “Don’t argue with me” — and from Rudy a handshake like a bench vise. From Father Osei, the holy card he left on the arm of the couch: Joseph with a sheaf of wheat, *Ite ad Ioseph*, which he explained at the door on his way out, in one sentence and a laugh — Pharaoh said it to the hungry, about the other Joseph, and it has never stopped being good advice.

body.title: An index card, typed
body.text: FIELD NOTE. St. Joseph is patron of workers, fathers, the dying, the Universal Church, and people trying to sell a house. You are at least two of these. —M.L.

body: On the couch Laney is reading his Facebook wall to Lena off her BlackBerry, because Lena gave up Facebook for Lent and is not allowed to look, and has her eyes shut to prove it: twenty-three people, his old CYO coach, and Becca Lindell, *birthdays count for a week at our house!!*, which Laney reads out with both exclamation points.
Lena brought his mail down from the desk at four and kept it, and hands it to him now. A big envelope from Glenwood Avenue in his mother’s writing, with a sheet of construction paper folded inside:

body.title: A drawing in crayon, from Glenwood Avenue
body.text: THIS IS JOSEPH. (St. Joseph, with a hammer and a carpenter’s square. At the bottom, unexplained, a crab.)

body: He studies the crab, and decides he will never ask Rosie about the crab as long as he lives.

And a small square envelope postmarked Breaux Bridge, with a card inside: a Joseph on the front in a printed gold frame, and pencil inside, an old woman’s pencil. Lena takes it out of his hands while he’s still working at the flap, and reads him one line, Mémère’s French in her mouth — “*Bonne fête au garçon de l’Ohio*” — and closes it, and puts it in her jean jacket. “For later.”
Last, she takes a bean from the bowl, one of Nonna’s, brown and flat, blessed with the rest of them before six, and holds out her other hand to him, palm up, for his wallet. He gives it to her.
“Keep one of these on you and you’re never broke a day,” she says. “Nonna’s orders. The Sicilians’ too.”

choices.text: “I’m a dishwasher. You’re going to need more beans.”
response: “It’s a *bean*, Youngstown, not a stimulus package.”
She tucks it in behind his driver’s license, where the State of Ohio can keep an eye on it, and hands the wallet back with a little slap into his palm. Paid in full.

choices.text: *Let her do it. Watch her do it.*
response: She does it carefully, as though the wallet were a missal: past his four dollars and his library card and the folded paper with the Glenwood numbers on it that he has never needed, until she finds the place behind his license, and slides the bean in there, and smooths the leather down over it with her thumb.
She gives it back to him. Her hand rests on top of the wallet, on top of his hand, and then it comes away.

choices.text: “Nonna mailed these to you, not me.”
response: “She did. I’m a bean courier now. It’s a very old order.”

She puts his bean behind his license. She takes a second one out of the bowl and drops it into the breast pocket of her own jean jacket, and buttons the pocket over it, looking at him while she does it.

s17.slug: FRIDAY · 11:48 PM · DELGADO HALL, HER LANDING — LE 19 MARS
body: Twelve minutes left of the nineteenth, by the RAZR lying open on the step. The building has gone quiet at last. The window on her landing is black glass with the stairwell in it — the tube light, the fire door, the two of them.

They came up at half past ten, when the Fishbowl was down to Laney asleep on a couch in her shower curtain and Kevin and Margot stacking the folding chairs, and Lena said she wanted to sit somewhere that didn’t smell of fish.

She’s on her step with her back to the cinderblock, in the jean jacket over a sweater, and socks: red wool ones, darned at one heel. The white ones are in her drawer. He is on the step below, sideways, the BIRTHDAY BOY sash rolled up beside him like a bandage, with a slab of Laney’s cake on a napkin that neither of them has touched since half past ten.

She takes Mémère’s card out of her jacket and opens it on her knee. She reads him the line again — “*Bonne fête au garçon de l’Ohio*” — and then the rest, in English, a sentence at a time, the pencil going up and down hill across the card, in something close to Mémère’s own voice, dry and level, a voice that has outlived most of the people who ever argued with it: “Happy birthday to the boy from Ohio. It is the day of Saint Joseph also, so you must share it, and he was here first. You were a good boy in my house but too thin. Eat what is put in front of you. Come back when the crawfish are fat. Odile Broussard.” She turns it to the light. “And then she drew a cross under her name, which means she’s praying for you, or that she doesn’t trust the post office. With her it’s both.”

body.text: She doesn’t put the card away. “On Ash Wednesday,” she says, “in the front room. She held on to that holy card with you and talked at you for a minute and a half, and I stood in the door and told you she said Joseph was a good man.”
body.else: She doesn’t put the card away. “She told me on the phone in February what she thought about Joseph,” she says. “I never passed it on.”

body: “She said Joseph never says a word. Not in all four Gospels. Not one. He has a dream and he gets up and does what he’s told, and that’s all we ever get out of him. And God trusted him with everything anyway. The girl, and the baby.” She looks at the card on her knee. “She said a man who can wait is worth ten who can talk. And then she said *that one*” — and Lena lifts her chin at him, from her step, as Mémère must have from the daybed — “*that one waits like a man who’s had practice.*”

body.text: “I didn’t translate that part,” Lena says. “I was holding a sweater.”
body.else: “I didn’t pass that part on,” Lena says. “I didn’t know what you’d do with it.”

body: He sits with that. Since August, every step of it, and an old woman in Breaux Bridge had it figured before he did.
He asks it now, finally. “Who told her?”
“I did.”

body.text: She says it to the card first, and then she looks up and says the rest to him. “At Christmas. On the phone to Breaux Bridge, the week I was deciding things.” She doesn’t say what things. He was in Youngstown that week, carrying his phone from room to room. “She asked me who I was thinking about so hard I’d let the roux burn, and I told her your birthday instead of your name. It was the only thing about you I could say out loud.”
body.else: She says it to the card first, and then she looks up and says the rest to him. “The night you told me. On the phone to Breaux Bridge, still mad at you for not telling me sooner.” She turns the card a little toward the light. “She’d been asking about you since Christmas, and I’d been answering about the weather. A birthday she could do something with.”

body: He doesn’t have anything to say to that. He reaches up and takes the hand that isn’t holding the card, and she gives it to him, and they sit that way, his elbow on her step, her fingers cold from the stairwell.

body.text: Brisk now, putting the card back in her jacket: “I’ll have you know this was very hard.” “The soup?” “*All* of it. Your grandmother writes in a code. Rudy’s oven is a liar. Laney wanted a *fog machine*.”
Brisk now, putting the card back in her jacket: “I’ve been thinking about the soup since Monday.” His own words, returned with the socks attached.
Brisk now, putting the card back in her jacket: “It cost a great deal more than five dollars.”
She puts the card back in her jacket and doesn’t say anything about the soup, or the oven, or any of it.

body: The phone on the step says 11:58 when she leans down off her step and kisses him.

It isn’t quick, and it isn’t in a hurry to become anything else. Both her hands come flat against his chest, on the canvas — the way she held him in place by the Hobart, one hand then, two now — and he waits for them to push, and they don’t; they stay, and press, and keep him exactly where she wants him. His hand goes into the hair at the back of her head, still stiff in one place with flour she missed, and the other settles at her waist, over the sweater, and stays there. She tastes of anise and coffee and Laney’s frosting. He wants her — the weight of her leaning down to him off the step, the warmth coming through the wool, the flour his thumb finds behind her ear — and under all of it there’s an order to it, and he can feel it. Her first. Then the wanting, after her, where it belongs, glad to be there. His hands stay where they are, and he doesn’t have to make them.
The phone turns over to 12:00. She sits back on her step, her hands still where they were, and her hair is a ruin, and she has never looked so pleased with herself.
“It’s not your birthday anymore,” she says. “I don’t kiss commoners.”

choices.text: “Best birthday I’ve had since I was a kid.”
choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you told Lena it was the best one you’d had since you were a kid.
response: She doesn’t make a joke of it. Over them the tube light flickers and steadies.
“It was supposed to be,” she says.

She takes her hands back and gets up and goes down the half flight to two in her red socks. At the wired glass she turns round with the door half open and looks up at him, and whatever she was going to say, she keeps.

choices.text: “At Christmas I was with —”
choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you reminded Lena who you’d been with at Christmas, and she said she’d told her grandmother your birthday anyway.
response: “I know who you were with,” Lena says. “I told her anyway.”
It isn’t a reproach. It’s a fact she has kept since December, and she hands it to him level, as you’d hand somebody a full cup.
She had started to get up. She sits back down on her step instead, and pulls the red socks up over her heels, and settles her back against the cinderblock for one more minute of Saturday.

choices.text: “You could have just asked me when it was.”
choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you told Lena she could have just asked you when your birthday was, and she said she hadn’t known there was anything to ask.
response: “I didn’t know there was anything to ask.” She looks at the card on her knee. “That’s what I was mad about. Not the birthday. That I had to find it out.”
She had started to get up. She sits back down on her step instead, and pulls the red socks up over her heels, and settles her back against the cinderblock for one more minute of Saturday.

choices.text: *Say nothing. Let it be Saturday.*
choices.key: When your birthday ended on her landing, you said nothing and let it be Saturday.
response: They sit. She lays her head on his shoulder, on the Carhartt, long enough for the RAZR’s little screen to give up and go dark on the step.

She gets up at last, and going past him she touches the top of his head, lightly, testing a loaf, and goes down the half flight in her red socks, and the door to two sighs shut on its closer. He stays on her step with the dark phone and the rolled-up sash, under the tube light, and it’s Saturday.

s18.slug: SATURDAY · 10:00 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — BREAKING THE TABLE
body: The Fishbowl is full of sun, all four glass walls of it, and the altar is still standing in the middle of the room, two thirds eaten. The lilies opened the rest of the way overnight and dropped their pollen down the top tier. On the bottom tier somebody has eaten every stuffed artichoke but one, and that one has a plastic fork standing straight up in it like a flag on a summit.

Lena has a clipboard. It has a pen tied to it with kitchen string and a list on it in her capitals, and she is running the room off the list in sweatpants and a black-and-gold Saints T-shirt with the Super Bowl date on the back. The food goes down the hill to the poor; it was always going to. The table was St. Joseph’s, she told the room last night with an artichoke in her hand, and St. Joseph gives everything away by Saturday noon.

Laney is labeling. She has a roll of masking tape and a Sharpie, and the bags come off the line with their contents announced in pageant capitals: BREAD (STAFF). BREAD (CROSS). BREAD (BEARD??). Margot is counting every loaf, lemon and cookie onto a legal pad in columns, for reasons she has not shared. Kevin is wrapping. He has the plastic wrap from the second-floor kitchen and does each loaf the same way, tight, the ends folded under in two neat triangles, and when Laney tells him it’s bread, Kevin, it isn’t going to sue anybody, he holds one up for her inspection.
“Respectfully, that’s a hospital corner.”

Theo is horizontal. He is on the couch they shoved back against the glass last night to make room for the saints, in last night’s shirt and a pair of sunglasses he has not taken off since he came in, with one forearm over the sunglasses for extra dark, and he contributes from there.
“Open on a glass room. A man wakes up surrounded by bread. He doesn’t know how he got there. Neither does the bread.”
“You ambulated in at eight-forty,” Margot says, writing. “Largely vertical.”
“Wake me when it’s spring.”
“Spring starts at ten thirty-two. I have it in writing.”

Jack’s job is the big loaves. The cross and the staff are too long for any bag Laney owns, so he breaks them over the foosball table into pieces a person could carry home, and the crust goes off like kindling and showers the little wooden men. When he reaches for Ohio, Lena takes it out of his hands.

It’s the loaf from the second tier, the size of a dinner plate, the shape of the state if you were generous about the bottom, a little too dark along Lake Erie where Rudy’s oven runs hot at the back. Laney has a strip of tape ready. Lena puts the loaf behind her.
“That one’s not for the poor. That one’s *evidence*.”

She wraps it herself in a clean dish towel and sets it on the windowsill, above the reach of everybody. From the end of the cross, before it goes into a bag, she breaks a piece the size of a matchbook, folds it into a paper napkin and holds it out to him.
“Mémère keeps a piece in the kitchen for hurricanes. You don’t have hurricanes. Keep it anyway.”

He puts it away inside the Carhartt. She watches it go in, and nods, and eats the last corner of Laney’s sheet cake for breakfast standing up, with her fingers, announcing to the room that on Friday she is back on bread and water and intends to be insufferable about it.
Last, she opens Celeste’s Royal Dansk tin, which has eleven of the four dozen left in it, and counts six fig cookies into a napkin and folds the napkin into a packet as neat as a field dressing.
“For the opposition.” She holds it up. “Somebody take these up to Hale. Not me. He’ll think I’m gloating.”
“You *are* gloating,” says Laney, taping.
“That’s why it can’t be me.”

The rest goes down Ocean Road. St. Brendan’s feeds whoever comes on Saturdays at half past eleven, in the parish hall under the church, and Lena has told them to expect bread. Eight bags stand by the glass doors with the cookie packet on top of the last one. She pulls her hair back into an elastic with both hands, picks up the first two bags, and turns round to see what he’s carrying.

choices.text: *Carry the bread down Ocean Road with her to the Saturday meal at St. Brendan’s.*
choices.key: The morning after your birthday, you carried the altar’s bread down to St. Brendan’s with Lena and served it.

choices.text: *Take the opposition’s fig cookies up to Hollis. He’ll be there; he always is on Saturdays.*
choices.key: The morning after your birthday, you took Lena’s fig cookies up to Professor Hale.

s19h.slug: SATURDAY · 11:30 AM · HOLLIS HALL, 314 — PATRON OF A HAPPY DEATH
body: Hollis on a Saturday is a building with the sound turned off. The stairwell lights are on a timer that hasn’t heard about weekends, so Jack climbs to three through a half dark with Lena’s napkin of fig cookies held level in front of him, past the bulletin boards, past a mop bucket left at the second landing with its mop standing in it at attention.

HALE, in gold leaf, flaking, on the pebbled glass. The door is open. Inside it’s the green carpet and the wine stain shaped like Italy, and Bishop Berkeley asleep across the boot of it with his gray muzzle on his paws; the books in their floor stacks; the radiator on, though it’s March and the sun is out; the Pacific filling the middle window right up to the frame. Hale is at the desk in a cardigan going at the elbows with a stack of 109H essays at his left hand and the fountain pen moving, and he doesn’t stop it when Jack knocks on the open door.
“If it’s about the grade, Mr. Costigan, it’s Saturday. I’m only cruel on weekdays.”
“It’s cookies. From the opposition.”
The pen stops.

Hale holds out a hand without getting up. Jack puts the napkin in it. Hale unfolds it on top of somebody’s essay and looks at the six of them — the white icing, the sprinkles, the slit across the top where the fig shows through — and takes one, and eats it at once, entire, in two bites, with real pleasure, and brushes the crumbs off a paragraph about Sebastian Flyte.

“Fig. Sicilian, or Calabrian. I shan’t ask which; she’d tell me, and it would take the afternoon.” He folds the napkin back over the other five, gently, the way a man covers a sleeping thing. “Miss Broussard is my best student and my worst defeat, and I intend to keep her for both.”
He looks at Jack properly, over the essays, the long look.

“And it was your birthday. Don’t look like that; I was told. I walked the dog past your dormitory last night at six. Bishop Berkeley is stone deaf, and even he heard Louis Prima. A boy on the front steps with a paper plate told me whose birthday it was and offered me a stuffed artichoke, which I declined, as it was plainly the property of the poor.” He picks the pen up again. “Nineteen. A dreadful age. I was insufferable at nineteen. I’m told I’ve improved.”
“Who told you that?”
“Nobody. That’s why I believe it.”

He taps the stack of essays with the end of the pen. “Twelve undergraduates on whether Sebastian Flyte is happy at Oxford. Eleven of them say yes, at length. One says he is happy the way you are happy at a party you know is ending, and I shall give that one an A and never tell her why.” He glances at the napkin. “Was there a priest? At this altar of hers.”
“Father Osei blessed it.”

“Of course he did. Your Father Osei would bless a parking meter if it held still long enough, and the meter would come away the better for it.” He says it with something very near affection, and goes back to the margin.
“It was St. Joseph’s too,” Jack says.
“So I gathered. One could see the bread from the street.” Hale turns the pen end over end on the blotter. “Husband. Carpenter. Patron of a happy death. My father would have liked him.”

He writes something in the margin of the essay under the cookies, with a question mark after it, and blots it. On the carpet Bishop Berkeley sighs in his sleep and stretches one long leg out across the Adriatic.

body.text: “And the parked car,” Hale says, without looking up from the margin. “Was it accepted?”
“It’s being argued. Wednesdays.”
One of Hale’s eyebrows goes up and comes down again with no question attached to it, and he moves on to the next sentence of the essay.

body: At the bottom of the page he caps the pen and sets it down crossways on the stack, and rests one hand on the napkin, to keep it from wandering off.
“Why did she send them?”

choices.text: “Because she’s kind.”
response: “She is.” Hale says it to the window. “It’s her most dangerous quality. Tell no one I said so.”
His hand, which has been resting on the napkin, comes away from it with a second cookie in it, and he eats that one looking out at the Pacific.

choices.text: “Because she won.”
response: “Yes. Gloating with baked goods.” He unfolds the napkin and inspects the five survivors. “Very Catholic. The Anglicans send a card.”
And Hale laughs — the short one, the Yorkshire one, all the Oxford knocked off it — and the dog on the carpet doesn’t hear a thing.

choices.text: “Because she wants a rematch.”
response: “She shall have one. October. I’ve told them.”

He pulls the blotter toward him and writes it there in green ink, in his backward-leaning hand, *Broussard — Oct.*, and underlines it, as if he might otherwise forget. Then he sits back with his fingers laced over the cardigan and looks out the middle window at the sea, pleased with October.

s19l.slug: SATURDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S PARISH HALL — THE LINE
body: The parish hall is under the church, down a flight of concrete steps beside the rectory: a long low room with a drop ceiling and its windows up at sidewalk height, so that all through the meal the people eating it can watch the ankles of Ocean Road go past. Folding tables in two rows. A steam table borrowed from the Knights. A coffee urn the size of a fire hydrant. On the end wall, hung a little crooked, a framed woodcut of Christ standing in a breadline among men in caps; Lena told him on the steps it’s a Catholic Worker print, and that she has straightened it twice and someone always puts it back.

By noon the line is out the door and up the steps, and Lena is behind the steam table in an apron that says KNIGHTS OF COLUMBUS COUNCIL 4115, and she is a different woman again. Jack has watched her take a room apart with Aquinas. He has never watched this. She knows everybody’s name. *Morning, Ray. Morning, Pilar, how’s the hip. Big Tom, Little Tom* — who aren’t related, and aren’t big or little, and have been Big Tom and Little Tom so long that neither of them remembers which came first. She knows who takes no onions and who takes two rolls and puts one in his coat for later, and the second roll is on that tray before he has to ask.

A man named Lyle comes through holding his tray in both hands. He is sixty or so, in a corduroy jacket buttoned one hole off over a flannel shirt with a breast pocket, and he has a beard he trims himself in a mirror that isn’t straight. Lena puts bread from the cross on his tray, and then, out of her apron pocket, a fava bean, brown and dry and hard as a coat button.

“That’s from St. Joseph, Lyle. One year in Sicily it didn’t rain, and the people prayed to him, and the only thing that came up out of the ground was these. They say if you carry one, you’ll never be broke.”
Lyle looks at the bean in his palm. “Never?”
“That’s what they say. I don’t answer for what they say.”
He puts it in the breast pocket of the flannel shirt, and then, with the tray balanced on one forearm, he buttons the pocket.

Two trays later a woman in a Raiders cap, who keeps an eye through the window on the shopping cart she left on the sidewalk, tells Lena she lost her reading glasses on the bus Thursday and she’s got St. Anthony working on it.
“Ask Joseph,” Lena says. “It’s his weekend. He found a twelve-year-old boy in the Temple, in Jerusalem, at Passover, with the entire country in town.”
“After three *days*,” the woman says. “Anthony’d have had it by lunch.”
Lena stands there with the ladle. The line behind the woman has stopped to hear how it comes out.
“She’s right,” Lena tells the line. “Y’all heard her. It’s Anthony. I take it back.” And she puts an extra fig cookie on the woman’s tray, for the trouble of being right.

Jack is on the dish sink in the kitchen behind the pass-through, sleeves pushed up, the sprayer bucking on its spring in his hand, and from there he can see her the whole time — the ladle, the names, the second roll before anybody asks — and he scrubs the same sheet pan twice and keeps what he sees to himself.

At ten past one the line is down to stragglers. Lena comes back through the swinging door with an empty bread tray and drops it in his sink. She rinses her hands under his faucet, and then, without drying them, puts one wet hand on the back of his neck and kisses him. The water runs down inside his collar. She tastes like the Knights’ coffee. Out in the hall somebody drops a bin of silverware and the room applauds, as church basements have always applauded a dropped tray, and she laughs against his mouth and doesn’t move away for it.

choices.text: “You’re good at this.”
response: “It’s not a talent. It’s a habit.” She dries her hands on the Knights’ apron at last. “You do a thing enough Saturdays, and the thing starts doing you.”
She picks up a tray of cuccidati off the counter, hits the swinging door with her hip, and is back out at the line with it, already calling somebody by name.

choices.text: “Lyle’s going to win the lottery now.”
response: “Lyle’s going to win the *Pick 3*.” She flicks water at him off her fingers. “Don’t be greedy for him.”
Through the pass-through, at the second table from the end, Lyle has finished his soup. He sits back, and pats the buttoned pocket twice, to make sure, and goes on with his bread.

choices.text: *Wash. Let her talk to Lyle.*
response: He turns back to the sink. She takes two cups of the Knights’ coffee out to Lyle’s table, and through the pass-through, over the sprayer, he can hear the two of them settle into the Saints’ offseason — who they ought to keep now they’ve won it, who they can let walk, whether Brees has another one in him — for twenty minutes, while he washes every pan in the parish.
When he looks up again, she has gone through the line herself with a tray and is sitting down across from Lyle with her own plate.

s20.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — VEILED
body: The purple is back, and there’s more of it than there was. Somebody has been up a stepladder since Friday. The crucifix over the altar has gone under a fall of purple cloth tied at the foot, and so have most of the statues, and over by the side altar, two days after his feast, so has St. Joseph, with Friday’s lilies still in a bucket at his feet and his face covered like the rest. Of all of them that’s the one Jack can’t stop looking at: two days ago the man stood at the top of three milk crates in a frame with everybody Jack knows eating underneath him, and this morning he has gone under the purple with the rest.

The altar society did it yesterday afternoon, Lena tells him in a whisper as they kneel: four women and a ladder, with Father Osei holding the ladder. It’s St. Brendan’s own custom, older than anybody in the society: every year, the Saturday before this Sunday, whatever anybody says, and they will not be talked out of it.

Kevin is in the pew in front of them in his good jacket, and Laney is beside him, in a hat — a real one, navy, with a brim — that she must have brought from Dallas for exactly this kind of emergency. She has her arm through his for the entrance hymn. Kevin, by all appearances, has decided not to notice. Up in the loft, under Gus, there’s a violin today: Clare Dominguez, with the band kids.

There’s no Gloria; Friday’s has been put away again with the white. Isaiah is about the Lord who made a road through the sea, telling his people to stop looking back at the old things, because he is doing something new. The psalm is the one about the people who went out weeping, carrying their seed, and came home singing with their sheaves, and the violin comes in under it, and in the pew in front Kevin doesn’t look up. Paul tells the Philippians he is forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead; Lena has that one by heart and moves her lips with the lector.
Then Father Osei reads John.

Early in the morning, in the Temple. The scribes and the Pharisees bring him a woman and stand her in the middle of everybody, and tell him what Moses said to do with women like her, and ask him what he says. And he bends down and writes on the ground with his finger. For as long as he’s writing, Jack is in Trumbull; then the scribes are at it again, and Jack is in the pew. Jesus straightens up and tells them, *Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her*, and bends down and goes on writing. And they go away one by one, beginning with the elders, until he’s alone with her, in the middle, where they left her standing.
Father Osei closes the book and comes down to the step and folds his hands over it.
“We are not told what he wrote in the dirt. I have always thought each of them read his own name there, and that is why the old ones left first.”
He goes back to his chair. Gus lets the quiet run a good long count before anybody stands for the Creed, and then the church gets to its feet in the purple.

At the sign of peace Lena turns to him and gives him her hand. Where her thumb presses the back of his, there’s something that isn’t her thumb: a blister, round and tight and shiny, the size of a lentil, on the pad of it. A burn. He looks down at it, and she sees him look.
“Peace be with you,” he says.
“Five a.m.”

He turns her hand over in his to see it properly, and she leaves it with him until the Lamb of God, and then takes it back and folds it into the other one, with the thumb tucked inside, out of sight, where it’s nobody’s business but hers, and sings.

s21.slug: SUNDAY · 7:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL — THE VOTE
body: The milk crates have gone back to whoever milk crates belong to, and the basement door has gone back to the basement, and the couches have been dragged home to their dents in the carpet. The Fishbowl is the Fishbowl again, except for one lily, the last of Friday’s, standing in a 7-Eleven Big Gulp cup of water on top of the television. On the television is C-SPAN.

Half the floor is in for it. Margot is at the coffee table with her laptop open and a *Tide* press pass on a lanyard she doesn’t need in her own lounge. Theo is at the foosball table with the coffee can from the Oscar pool, running a book on the margin — a dollar a guess, closest takes the can — and he has no opinion about the bill at all except that it is the best television since the Academy Awards. Yusuf is in for a dollar on seven. Kevin is on the arm of the couch with his BlackBerry face down on his knee. Laney is cross-legged on the rug, furious with every single person on the screen on principle, by name and state.

This afternoon Stupak and his holdouts went in front of the cameras and said they’d vote yes, now that the President had agreed to sign an executive order on the abortion money. Since then the vote has been a formality the networks keep calling a cliffhanger.

Lena came in at seven with her arms folded and hasn’t unfolded them. She started at the far end of the couch from Jack, and as the clock runs down she isn’t at the far end anymore; a person needs somebody to be angry next to. She wanted the bill. She wanted it with Stupak’s language nailed into it, the way he swore in November it would be, and she believed him.

“An executive order,” she says, to Jack, as though he wrote it. “It’s a press release with a seal on it.” She jabs a thumb at the laptop on the coffee table, where Margot has both letters open in tabs. “The sisters and the bishops. I’ve agreed with both of them since Wednesday, and I think I’ve pulled something.”

Jack has been against it since the summer and has said so at this coffee table more than once: two thousand pages; a trillion dollars that hasn’t been found yet; Washington telling a man in Campbell to buy insurance or pay a fine; and the funding language, which he has read, and she has read, and they read differently.
“It’s a bad bill with a good reason on top of it,” he says.
“It’s a good reason with a bad bill underneath. Those are different animals. I grew up three miles from Charity Hospital, Jack. I know what the poor get when the answer is *later*.”
“I grew up in Youngstown. Washington’s been coming to save us since 1977. We’ve got some beautiful studies.”

“Oh, don’t. Don’t do the mill at me.” She unfolds one arm to point at him and folds it back. “Your side had the White House and both houses and didn’t lift a finger for a waitress in Chalmette with diabetes and no doctor.”
“They’re not my side. They’re the ones I’d sit with.”
“Then go sit with them,” she says, and doesn’t move away from him to say it.
On the screen the yeas climb in a box in the corner of the picture.

Theo goes round with the can a last time. Kevin waves him off. He is for the bill, quietly; when Laney twists round on the rug and demands to know whether anybody in this room has a spine, he says, without raising his voice, “My mom’s counter at the Walgreens in San Jose. Guy put his insulin back because he couldn’t pay for it, and bought Doritos.” He says nothing more, and nobody asks him to.
Margot swivels the laptop a quarter turn without looking away from the screen. “Broussard. I need a pro-life Democrat for the *Tide*. On the record.”
“Put *Catholic, furious, anonymous*.”
“That isn’t a quote.”
“It is in Louisiana.”

Two hundred and sixteen is the number. Margot says so, typing. The yeas go to two hundred and ten, to two hundred and fourteen, to two hundred and sixteen, and the floor of the House makes a sound like a ballpark.
“Told you,” Jack says.
“Not a word,” says Lena.
At a quarter to eight the gavel comes down on 219 to 212.

Margot types, stops, types. “I’m writing *historic* in brackets until I decide how I feel.” Theo counts the can out into Yusuf’s hand — seven on the nose — and Yusuf folds the bills in half and says a structure never gives where you’re looking; it gives at the joints. And Laney, who has been furious at everybody on C-SPAN for forty minutes including the stenographer, is crying a little at the number, and wipes it with the heel of her hand, and says it’s the lily. It’s pollen. She’s been allergic to lilies since Friday.

Lena has a hand over her mouth. When she takes it away she says, at the television, “Thirty-two million people,” and then, “and *that*,” and doesn’t finish either one. Her eyes are wet and her chin is up and she turns on the couch to face him, like she’s daring him to be right.

choices.text: *An executive order can be torn up with a pen. You can’t vote for a law on a promise.*
choices.key: When the House passed the health-care bill, you told Lena an executive order could be torn up with a pen, and she said that was exactly why she was angry.
response: “I *know*. That’s why I’m *angry*. Not because you’re right.”
She takes the nearest cushion — orange corduroy, older than either of them — and throws it at him from a foot and a half, accurately, in the face. Theo, at the foosball table, applauds the form.

When they start voting on the fixes she is still beside him, arms folded so tight her elbows have gone white, glaring at the new count, ready to throw a cushion at that too, with her knee against his throughout.

choices.text: “Thirty-two million people get a doctor. I can’t sneer at that.”
choices.key: When the House passed the health-care bill, you granted Lena that thirty-two million people getting a doctor was nothing to sneer at.
response: It stops her halfway into a sentence about Michigan.
“No,” she says. “You can’t.”

It makes her angrier, visibly — at having to hold both halves at once, at him for handing her the one she didn’t want handed — and she starts again about the funding language and gets as far as “Section thirteen-oh-three —” and loses the thread of it, and kisses him instead, hard and short, to end the sentence.
When she pulls back she is still scowling at C-SPAN.

choices.text: “Your party just cut a deal with a Catholic from Michigan over a piece of paper. Welcome to my world.”
choices.key: When the House passed the health-care bill, you welcomed Lena to your world, and she reminded you it had Ohio in it.
response: “*Your* world has *Ohio* in it.”
She kisses him, quick, on the mouth, the way she’d slap a table to make a point, and sits back with her arms folded again.
From the foosball table, rattling the empty can: “Is that a concession?”
“It’s a *point of order*.”

choices.text: “I hate that your own side did this to you. I’d hate it if it were mine.”
choices.key: When the House passed the health-care bill, you told Lena you hated that her own side had betrayed her.
response: She looks at him a long time, with the blue of the television down one side of her face.
“It *will* be yours one day,” she says. “Remember you said that.”

She puts her head on his shoulder. The second vote starts, the fixes, and the box in the corner of the screen begins to count again, and she watches it with him without a word, her head on his shoulder the whole way down.

s22.slug: SUNDAY · 9:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, HER STEP — SOMETHING NEW
body: On a Sunday night the stairwell has the hum of the building in it and nothing else. Jack is on her step tonight, on the landing between two and three, under the black window, with the four-dollar Catechism open on his knee to thirty-nine; and Lena is on the step below him, still angry. She has been angry since lunch and sees no reason to stop because a vote is over. She leans back against his shins anyway.
The RAZR buzzes. It’s past midnight in Youngstown; his father has sat up for the fixes.

body.text: PASSED. YOUR MOTHER SAYS GOOD. I SAY WE’LL SEE. STUPAK SHOULD HAVE HELD.

body: Lena twists round and reads it over his arm.
“Your father agrees with me.”
“My father agrees with you *and* my mother. Don’t make him pick.”
She weighs that, with her chin up, and appears to allow it, and leans back again.
He writes his father back and puts the phone away.

“Mémère’s going to call me tomorrow and ask why I sound sad,” Lena says, “and I’m going to have to explain the House of Representatives to her in French.” She thinks about it. “She’ll take Stupak’s side. She’ll say he has an honest face. And then she’ll ask if I’m going Thursday, for the Annunciation, and I’ll say yes, and that’ll be the only part she listens to.”

Between them on the step, in its dish towel, is Ohio. She brought it up from 217 under her arm and hasn’t said why. Now she unwraps it on her knees. Three days old, it has gone hard enough to knock on, and she breaks a corner off the top right, the lake corner — Ashtabula, Jack thinks, give or take — and breaks that in half and hands half up to him, and wraps the rest of the state back up, the heel and all, and keeps it. It tastes of anise and Rudy’s oven. It takes some chewing.
“I had a stone in my hand,” she says, when she can. “I just couldn’t decide who to throw it at.”
He eats his half of Ashtabula.

When the bread is gone she reaches up behind her and tips the book down off his knee to where she can see it, and reads him the heading, round and careful: “*How Can We Speak about God?*” And then the first line, the same way, all the way to the end of it: the Church’s confidence that it’s possible to speak about him to everyone and with everyone — other religions, philosophy, science. And then the end of it again in her own voice, low, only for the two of them: “*With unbelievers and atheists.*”
She slides the book back up to his knee.
“Wednesday,” she says, and tips her head back against his knee.
